en: The Scripture on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the land established by the Tathāgatas, extolling the Dharmakāya.
Profound and delightful, they universally beheld pavilions that were grandly adorned and pure, radiant palaces of majestic power, and treasuries of lapis lazuli—the domain where the Tathāgatas act.

At that time, the Buddha manifested immeasurable paths as palaces of the Dharma-realm; he beheld the bodhisattvas’ bodies, their radiance pure, upon lion thrones, all of which served as great Dharma-thrones embodying the forms of all bodhisattvas.

They extol the holy intent of the Tathāgatas throughout the dharma-realm; taking the realm of empty space as their condition, they act without hindrance, clearly understanding the realm of the holy wisdom of the ultimate limit, universally comprehending the Buddha-wisdom, and discerning the noble path.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present are all entirely equal, constituting a single Dharma-body;
the practices of all Buddhas are equally uniform, and their practice of supernormal powers is free from all obstruction.
The Dharma-body is the essence of wisdom, ultimately signless;

the Dharma-measure is infinite, roaming through the Dharma-realm without dualistic conduct. Being profound, vast, and limitless, it constitutes supreme perfect enlightenment. Its equality is like that of a scale, whereby one transcends the practices of conditioned existence; there are no aggregates or hindrances, for this is the gateway to liberation.
That Dharma-realm is universally identical to empty space;
it constantly traverses the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and because it is limitless, there is nowhere it does not behold.

There are hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, all of whom are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Each resides in a different Buddha-world, possessing infinite aspirations and practicing various acts of wisdom, each entering the indestructible, equal Dharma-realm.
The realm of space is infinite; it is without attainment, without intermediate activity, without inherent existence, and without arising.
To clearly understand and realize that all phenomena are likewise is to be enlightened.

The bodies of the assembly of bodhisattvas remained unmoved and detached; they attained all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, pervading all buddha-lands without conceptualization, and by following the wisdom of the Tathāgata, they now attained the manifest radiance of the Buddha-way.

Wandering through the practices of the Great Sage without being shaken, he uses wisdom to manifest a single body throughout the infinite; the substance of his conduct pervades the interior of the boundless Dharma-realm, distinguishing the realms of virtuous people and sentient beings until they reach the stage of non-retrogression.

Equally attaining the fundamental limit and the dharma-realm of no-dharmas, they eliminate self-conceit; with bodies always humble and compliant, they have nothing to fear, as the Tathāgata illuminates all roots of virtue to serve as their companions.
Their names were:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantaghoṣeśvara Bodhisattva, Tathāgatakulasaṃbhavacūḍa Bodhisattva, Vajraketudhvaja Bodhisattva, Anāvaraṇacandraprabha Bodhisattva, Sūryaprabhāmalanidhi Bodhisattva, Mahāṛddhivikurvaṇa Bodhisattva, Vimalaprabhāmukuṭa Bodhisattva, Daśadigvīryarāja Bodhisattva, and Mahāsiṃhavikrīḍitarddhi Bodhisattva.
Such as these, the number of bodhisattvas in the assembly was like the countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of dust motes that fill the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

Then there was a light called the "Noble Intent of the Tathāgata," which the World-Honored One emitted from between his eyebrows; this radiance shone throughout immeasurable, boundless, and limitless worlds in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. It manifested the majestic spiritual transformations of the Tathāgata and addressed an incalculable multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas. Through its majestic power, it caused all evil realms in all Buddha-worlds to be utterly extinguished and eclipsed all the palaces of the māras.

Furthermore, when all Tathāgatas attain supreme perfect enlightenment, they awaken those who have not yet awakened; they manifest the assembly halls and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Buddhas, emitting rays of light that illuminate the Dharma-realm and the supreme realm of space, pervading everywhere throughout all Buddha-fields. These rays then return, circling the seats of all Bodhisattvas, and enter the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Saṃkusumitarājendra of the Tathāgata lineage, where they do not reappear.
Thus, all the bodhisattvas in the assembly were struck with unprecedented wonder, their bodies and minds leaping with joy:
"Today there shall be an infinite transformation as the Great Dharma is expounded; such radiance has appeared spontaneously."

As soon as the light had vanished, the Bodhisattva Śiribhadra of the Tathāgata clan rose from his seat, descended with his right knee upon the lotus flower, knelt down with palms joined, and contemplating the virtues of the Tathāgata, he praised him in verse:
Awakening those who were not yet awakened, Surpassing all kings of virtue, His conduct is without obstruction; Such is the arising of his *pāramitās*.
That Great Sage abides in peace, equal toward the three periods of time;
I now bow my head in reverence to this wise and enlightened sage.
His conduct is free from form or sign, and thus he has crossed to the further shore.
Furthermore, he manifests a body beautifully adorned;
its radiance is free from all defilement and displays hundreds of thousands of beams of light.
Having subdued all demonic activities, I bow my head in refuge and pay homage to him.
Shaking all the lands, the foremost of palaces,
and even throughout the ten directions— all the existing territories—
he shall never cause a single person to experience fear.
The majestic spiritual power of the Buddha-way is such as this;
it is established with equanimity throughout the realm of empty space.
Such is the Dharma-realm, whereby one attains all buddha-fields.
He purifies the masses, as numerous as the atoms of billions of worlds;
he eliminates all the sins and transgressions of every sentient being.
His vow is exceedingly firm and strong, and he practices it throughout billions of kalpas.
By practicing and accumulating virtue, one attains the extraordinary path of the Buddha.
Upon reaching the state of the Single Practice, noble wisdom becomes unimpeded;
through the spontaneity of this Oneness, one practices all the paths of the Buddhas.
The light he emanates and radiates—such is the Teacher;
it is seen throughout the entire Sahā world, reaching everywhere without exception.
He universally manifests all the transformations of his majestic spiritual power.
My body has already attained entry into this single natural practice.
For this reason, I have now given rise to this thought:
"Now is the truly appropriate time; I bow my head to the Dharma King."
Countless bodhisattvas have all gathered here,
desiring to hear and examine the Dharma matters that are being distinguished.
Those assembled today are pure, and yet even more pure.
Throughout all worlds, they draw near to and practice in accordance with them.
Their noble wisdom is immeasurable, their sphere of activity is unimpeded,
and they have attained courageous vigor and infinite majestic spiritual power.
These beings wander through the world with spiritual kinship; their conduct reaches that of the immortals.
Their wisdom is incalculable, and they transcend the power of diligence.
They produce a vigorous radiance that illuminates all bodhisattvas.
Now, as a humble person, I ask:
"What is the sphere of activity for this most excellent and supreme Dharma?
May the Great Sage, through his supernatural powers, freely manifest its majestic brilliance and reveal it everywhere.
"O Supreme Honored One, Teacher!
Proclaim which among the Buddha-fields is the one where the Sage among Men resides—the most supreme true son.

Having spoken these verses of praise, at that moment the World-Honored One emitted from his mouth a light called "Incalculable Billions of Illuminations," which shone upon all boundless Buddha-worlds. It circled those Buddha-fields ten times, manifesting the sacred will and majestic transformations of the Tathāgata. It summoned countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas so that they might all behold and receive his command. It shook the Buddha-fields and reached into all evil realms, completely extinguishing their calamities and afflictions, while eclipsing all the palaces of the Māras.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, through their impartial and perfect enlightenment, awaken all that is unawakened and manifest the assembly and site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of all Buddhas.

The radiance of their light transcends the dharma-realm, pervading the entire realm of empty space; reaching all Buddha-lands, it immediately returns and circles the bodhisattvas before entering the face of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

As soon as Samantabhadra Bodhisattva encountered this light, his merit, majestic countenance, and lion throne immediately increased manifold according to the occasion—surpassing the Buddha’s body and lion throne, and moreover transcending the bodies and lion thrones of all other bodhisattvas.
The majestic appearance, virtuous qualities, and lion throne of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva were exceptionally sublime and appeared with extraordinary splendor.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kulaprabhāsa of the Tathāgata’s lineage asked Samantabhadra:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
The merit of your benevolence is inconceivable; it is known throughout all worlds.
You manifest great transformations to gladden the bodhisattvas, moving them to the utmost degree. Now, O Son of the Buddha!
"What is this marvelous omen manifested by the Tathāgata?
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said to the Bodhisattva Chief of the Tathāgata Lineage:

"As I recall it, and as was witnessed by all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of antiquity, when such infinite transformations and stirrings appear, one should preach the sūtra on the manifestation of the Tathāgata."
"Now, the Great Sage wishes to expound this meaning; therefore, he again manifests such transformations and responses.
As soon as the Bodhisattva Chengshou of the Tathāgata clan heard the name of this exalted and manifest scripture, the earth immediately shook violently through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śrīsaṃbhava of the Tathāgata lineage addressed Samantabhadra, saying:
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are well able and capable of joyfully extolling for the sake of all such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas the manifestation and accomplishment of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Now, all ten directions are entirely adorned and purified, and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of beings have gathered here.

Having long cultivated pure conduct in the past, their minds find refuge; they embrace virtue and the Way, manifest the aspiration for enlightenment, expound great words, and cross over to the other shore.

They establish all the practices, dignified conduct, and ritual etiquette of the Tathāgatas; they keep the Buddhas in mind without ever forgetting or abandoning them; and they give rise to great compassion, universally observing all sentient beings.

The great bodhisattvas have attained definitive mastery of supernatural powers and discern the diligence of all Tathāgatas; their own bodies are serene and tranquil as they hear the sounds of the Dharma praised by all Buddhas—the sublime and wondrous teachings.

Such are their virtues and reputations; they have impartially eliminated all hatred and attachment, remaining free from favoritism or aversion, and now these bodhisattvas have all gathered here in assembly.
You, O Benevolent One, as a son of the Buddha, have already made offerings to countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, bowing your head to receive their teachings;

you have fully practiced all the bodhisattva deeds, attained great supernormal powers, the various gateways of samādhi, and the playful mastery of supernatural faculties, and have entered the secret treasury of the Tathāgatas;
you have eliminated all doubts, entered the fearless diligence of the Tathāgata, and investigated and perceived the various faculties of all sentient beings.
All [these teachings] are expounded as sutras based on faith in the True Truth and liberation;
they penetrate the movements of the Tathāgata, proclaim all the dharmas of the Buddhas to which the noble nature returns, and are the foremost among the attainments of the Infinite Deliverance.
Such analogies are beyond measure, for his manifold virtues are most extraordinary.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!

I pray that you will speak of the Tathāgata’s manifestation and appearance, the far-reaching resonance of his voice, the various mental activities and spheres of experience he expounds, the practices he praises that lead to the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the proclamation of the Buddha's teachings, and the manifestation of great parinirvāṇa; and may you reveal all the roots of merit and the various deeds performed by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kulapravara, wishing once more to clarify the meaning and discern its ultimate destination, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra in verse:
"Excellent is the refuge that is free from conjunction; It is the thorough understanding and complete awakening.
That wisdom is unsurpassed, Equanimous and detached from the dust of desire."
Praising the Most Victorious One, whose conduct is immeasurable,
all who hear his voice leap for joy. How does this extraordinary Bodhisattva arise so preeminently?
By what means is one able to find refuge? By what cause is reality attained?
What is the resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice? What is meant by body and mind?
What is the sphere of his practice? And what is this great renown?
What is it that constitutes the Buddhas, and for what reason are they called Tathāgatas?
Why are they the most supreme, and why do they turn the wheel of Dharma?
I pray you explain how the multitudes may dwell in peace upon the ground of the path to nirvāṇa.
One should gladden these and all the infinite sons of the Buddhas who dwell throughout the ten directions—
those Great Dharma Kings who abide securely, the refuge for the merit of all sentient beings.
Regarding these blessings and auspiciousness, may the Great Sage please explain them for us:
by what causes does one perceive the intent of the Path,
and how does one attain abiding in peace?
How can one hear the name of the Tathāgata?
Having never before beheld the Great Sages who have entered parinirvāṇa,
if one should give rise to exultation and pay reverent homage to the Honored Sage.
Please speak of this with joy; by what cause is the Great Resolve accomplished?
I now ask you about this, O Great Man of Purification!
Pray explain that which is to be practiced, O Great Virtuous One, Ocean-like in depth.
Observing all these bodhisattvas, who have all joined their palms to question the Buddha and the Benevolent One, as well as to consult me,
for their sake I shall proclaim the Dharma of the Pure Honored One.
To sever the doubts of the multitude, And to attain immeasurable great wisdom,
He employs parables as a means, Manifesting the lineage of the Buddhas;
If sentient beings were to hear this, They would give rise to the pure mind of the Way.
They cause all Buddha-lands to be completely filled, without exception;
the Buddhas manifest everywhere in various kinds of physical forms.
Those who know the purity of the Dharma then expound it according to the appropriate time.
Based on their kinsmen as metaphors, he manifests and teaches them.
He travels to tens of millions of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions—
hundreds, thousands, billions, hundreds of nayutas in number, immeasurable and incalculable.
Bodhisattvas such as these, who are so difficult to encounter,
have gathered today in a manner as sovereign and sublime as this. Therefore,
I pray that you will explain how they dwell securely in pure conduct.
Through this, they widely proclaim and expound the lineage of the Tathāgata.
All these bodhisattvas stand with palms joined,
universally and wholeheartedly seeking the Dharma, thirsting for and yearning for the scriptures.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, having been questioned by Śikhaṇḍin—who was born into the lineage of the Tathāgata—addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O, sons of the Most Victorious!..."

When the Tathāgatas, the Inconceivable, the Truly Realized, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, appear in the world, they expound an immeasurable sequence of teachings that can never be fully calculated or measured.
The Tathāgata’s majesty and sublimity are thus; although he may employ a single matter, it is not by means of that single matter alone that he returns to the Way.
Why is this? Because he is solely designated by the title "Buddha."

Furthermore, there are ten matters that constitute the refuge of immeasurable dharmas and incalculable hundreds of thousands of merits; by practicing and cultivating these deeds, one attains the state of a Tathāgata.
What are these ten?
The mind of the Way is immeasurable, universally protecting the intentions of all sentient beings and the thoughts of their accumulated virtuous deeds from past lives;
its nature and disposition are boundless, being pure from the very beginning;
it gathers together infinite great kindness and great compassion, applying itself to the practice of rescuing and delivering all living beings.
May their vows and practices be bottomless, never ceasing as they cultivate infinite merit and wisdom;
may they practice without weariness and find their ultimate refuge therein;
and may they teach and transform sentient beings through the boundless treasury of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, they cultivate the path of purity that accords with the sublime truths;
the path of immeasurable skillful means and wisdom;
and the path of infinite virtue and boundless practice.
One gathers the accumulated noble wisdom and embraces the boundless treasury of the sūtras containing the meaning of the Dharma.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
the practice of these ten dharmas is the foremost of all dharmas.
Having fulfilled these ten, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of incalculable retinues and followers attained refuge in the Tathāgata.
"For example, O Son of the Buddha!
The designation 'thousand-world system' is not formed by a single factor, but is composed through the gathering of countless elements."
For example, when a great cloud does not miss its appointed season and pours down rain, there are four causes and conditions by which various winds blow gently, wafting and spreading [the rain]:
there is a wind named "The Controller" (*Ādāna*), whose great wind-field contains much water and governs the leading of the rain;
there is the "Drying Wind," which burns up the water.
There is a wind named "Abiding" (*sthiti*), which causes all palaces to abide;

there is a wind named "Adornment" (*vyūha*), which travels through the three thousandfold world-systems for the sake of sentient beings who experience the body [of rebirth] according to their merits and demerits.
The meritorious virtues accomplished by all these Bodhisattvas are likewise thus: they are without limit and cannot be calculated or measured;

they are like the various worlds established within a trichiliocosm that give rise to all dharmas—no one can distinguish or count them, weigh their beginning or end, nor can anyone perceive their ultimate source.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not arise for the sake of a single matter, nor for the sake of a single principle.

Furthermore, from the time of the former Tathāgatas in antiquity, he has first caused the vast rain of the Dharma to fall; his mind honors the teachings without weariness or fatigue, his will and nature are firm and strong, he maintains them without forgetting, he is free from confusion, and he observes with profound stillness.
By means of the site of wisdom, they exhaust all desires born of defilement; they exhort others to cultivate the roots of manifold virtues, skillfully establishing progress and eliminating arrogance.
Discriminatingly and decisively realizing the practice of purity, he expounds the verbal teachings to purify the virtues of all sentient beings.

The merit and power of the Tathāgata originate from the outflow-free (anāsrava) source; he embraces such ultimate truth and perfect enlightenment, attaining all dharmas. Within those, there is nothing that arises or emerges; this is the entry into the foremost gate, wherein the conduct of Bodhisattvas reaches the manifestation of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like this: suppose in the trichiliocosm a great cloud named 'Indestructible' naturally arises and flourishes, raining down at the appropriate time. Other lands would be unable to withstand or receive such water; only the trichiliocosm is capable of enduring the transformation of such waters."
Thus it is, O worthy one!

Within the Buddha’s Dharma-realm there is a vast and transformative grace called "Indestructible," which gathers together and ensures that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed; yet this is something that all noble beings, all śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are incapable of upholding or practicing.
"Only the Bodhisattvas, relying on great power, have minds free from fear and vow to don the armor of virtue; these are the two matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Listen clearly, throughout the ten directions, To all that is supreme in the world.
Seeking its peer, none can be found; it is likened unto empty space.
The conduct of the Guide is immeasurable and boundless;
thus it has no equal, for his virtues are all-pervasive.
Even if one were to contemplate the Buddha, the source of his mental recollections,
those who exist throughout the ten directions possess immeasurable merit.
Though the words from the mouths of all people were used to praise him for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, [it would still not suffice].
The Great Lion is infinite; in the mundane world there is no peer to him.
Throughout all the ten directions, in every Buddha-field that exists, even if they were all shattered into particles as fine as dust, and for as many eons as there are such particles—
Furthermore, even if hundreds of thousands of millions of beings from all ten directions were to offer praise,
they could not exhaustively describe the merit of a single hair-pore.
Suppose there were a man who wished to measure the entirety of space;
The second person’s calculation is thus: to swiftly calculate the characteristics of all sensations is impossible;
they are immeasurable and infinite, such that one could not exhaustively reach the limits of empty space.
One should know that throughout the ten directions, such practices are likewise boundless.
Even if all people of the three ages, all those dwelling within the triple world,
were to devise a plan to calculate the mental activities and thoughts of these sentient beings—
even for a single moment of the mind— their total number could be known.
The various thoughts of all living beings are what the conscious mind contemplates;
they are like the dharma-realm, entirely without limit or boundary,
yet one does not perceive any destination of that dharma-realm.
The Ten Powers are likewise; their activities are immeasurable.
All things are non-existent, for the Dharma-realm is its own nature.
It is like a great rain that falls, which is called "indestructible."
There is none capable of receiving it; only the calamity of water can encompass it.
The Buddha spreads his boundless grace, yet the Lesser Vehicle cannot bear it;
only the Bodhisattvas can receive and uphold it, extending it everywhere to all beings.
Non-arising is like non-arising; in stillness, there is no duality of thought.
That which is forever without birth is called universal equality.
Throughout all worlds, the objective realm is likewise thus.
Fundamentally non-existent and naturally so, already liberated from increase and decrease;
like this very limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the true limit of reality is itself boundless.
The three periods of time are equalized, universally liberating all.
Compassion such as this is the practice of the Guide;
it pervades all three periods of time, entirely without obstruction.
At the primordial limit there is nothing created; being uncreated, it is spontaneously so.
Inherently pure like space, it is without defilement or affliction.
Thus is the manifestation of the Most Victorious One: all things are entirely adorned and purified;
having already abandoned both the created and the uncreated, one casts aside the matters of existence and non-existence.
Releasing the sounds of speech and all resonant tones, he eliminates coming and going; in parinirvāṇa there is nothing that exists.
All things in the ten directions are thus; regarding the Dharma, they are spontaneous.
All speech is without sound, and it cannot be grasped or maintained.
Thus pure and tranquil, one understands all phenomena to be like the tracks of birds in the sky, or like a stone placed in empty space.
Relying on his original vows, he manifests a physical body;
observing all the ten directions himself, he is the supreme transformation of the Most Victorious One.
Even if one wishes to enter this most excellent realm, it is just like this.
One should resolve to follow the Way and purify one’s own will and nature.
Restraining and relinquishing all discursive thoughts, even regarding mindfulness there is no mindfulness;
like the tracks of a bird in the sky, such is the entry of the mind.
Therefore, Son of Peace!
Examine the conduct of the various guides and listen to what I say; I shall skillfully set forth various parables.
Even if one were to calculate throughout the ten directions, their fame and virtue would be inexhaustible.
How much more so when their meaning is explained, and one praises and lectures upon the Holy Honored One?
Just as those various classes of sentient beings naturally practice until they reach [enlightenment],
they are unable to conceive or calculate the conduct of all the Teachers.
The fruits of the realms of the ten directions, the sovereign assembly of the Buddha-way,
and the accomplishment of all roots of virtue— listen and hear of all these virtues.
Now appearing as a person in this world, contemplate and practice them until nothing remains.
Never having thought of capability, they gather together depending on causes and conditions.
Within ten billion lands there are words; their sounds combine in hundreds of billions.
Thus it is called the world of speech, established by reason of the three thousandfold world system.
The Supreme among Men is thus; all such qualities are naturally beyond calculation or description, even as they pervade his sphere of activity.
One could constantly proclaim them, yet they encompass the thoughts of all sentient beings.
The Honored One among Men is unknowable; his conduct is spontaneous and natural.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
Just as this rain comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, yet brings about this moisture;
These classes of sentient beings arise due to their transgressions and merits.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

These Tathāgatas who flourish in the transformation of the Way come from nowhere and go nowhere, yet they bring forth the rain of Dharma; all of this is due to the power of the fundamental virtues of the assembly of Bodhisattvas. These are the three matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as rain comes from nowhere, And likewise goes nowhere;
So too is the Buddha's transformation of all things: Neither coming nor going."
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is as if a great rain falls upon the trichiliocosm; no person capable of receiving it can calculate or know the number of its drops—even if all the sentient beings arising within a single buddha-field were to contemplate that vast bounty, their mental eyes would be confounded. Only the Lord knows: the Sovereign Deva-son fully knows the total number of drops in the rain falling upon the trichiliocosm, not missing a single one, all of which is brought about by the power of his past fundamental virtues."
Thus it is, O worthy one!

All sentient beings—whether śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—cannot comprehend, contemplate, or observe the Dharma-benefit of the Tathāgata; they cannot even conceive of or bring to mind his Great Resolve. Were they to hear of this Great Resolve, they would surely become bewildered.

Only the Bodhisattvas, the Honored Ones among sentient beings, who have well-cultivated their spiritual practices under past Buddhas and attained supreme power, are able to know it. This is the fourth [point].
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when there is a great rain, Pervading the three thousandfold world-system, Only the Honored Son of Heaven can discern it; No others are able to distinguish it."
"Consider all those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
they do not understand the rain of the Buddha-dharma, for only Bodhisattvas can know it.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
When the great clouds arise, there is also a rain called "Extinguishing," which completely extinguishes fire;
there is a great rain called "Confounding," which destroys the calamity of water;
and there is another great rain called "Severing," which cuts off and eliminates the wind.
Furthermore, there is a great rain called "Destruction," which ruins and destroys the great treasures;
there is also a great rain called "Decay," which causes the three thousandfold world system to rot and disintegrate.
The Tathāgata thus appears in the world, bringing forth the great rain of Dharma called "Extinguishing," which spreads the moisture of the Dharma to eliminate all worldly afflictions and desires;
it is also called "Accumulating," which spreads the moisture of the Dharma to accumulate the roots of all virtues;
and it is also called "Purifying," which spreads the moisture of the Dharma to sever all sixty-two views.
It is also called "Dissolving" as it expounds the flow of the Dharma, causing the wisdom of all dharmas to be perfected;
it is also called "Digesting" as it expounds the flow of the Dharma, transforming and extinguishing all mental activities—this is the fifth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as rain extinguishes fire, As rain destroys the calamity of water,
As rain cuts off the wind, And brings down the great mountain of jewels;”
The Tathāgata has appeared in the world, extinguishing all craving and accumulating the roots of myriad virtues;
he eliminates the sixty-two views and lets the rain of Dharma fall throughout the ten directions, bringing all wisdom to fulfillment.
Transforming the dispositions of sentient beings, Causing them to follow the True Path.
Enabling them not to be stingy with the four great elements, And realizing that the three realms have no fundamental origin;
Spontaneously attaining infinite compassion, And the three types of perfect knowledge without obstruction.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
Just as rain has a single taste, yet nourishes boundlessly and moistens everything everywhere;

so it is with the Tathāgata, who, through one great compassion, rains upon all beings to reach the infinite. The moisture of the Dharma is universal and pervasive, leading those who embrace it to the Great Sage. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata differentiates and manifests immeasurable dharmas; this is the sixth matter."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as rain, being of a single flavor, Pervades and moistens all things;
So too is the Tathāgata: His conduct is equal, without partiality or bias."
Then, with one great compassion, he rains down upon all people;
the moisture of the Dharma reaches the infinite, universally embracing them as they arrive at the Great Way.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is just as when the trichiliocosm undergoes reformation: first, the palaces inhabited by the sons of the gods in the form realm are formed; next, the dwellings of the people in the desire realm are formed; and finally, the various classes of sentient beings are brought into existence.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world in this manner, he first brings to fulfillment the wisdom of all bodhisattvas; thereafter, he sequentially expounds the wisdom and conduct of pratyekabuddhas; next, he reveals the wisdom practiced by those who have cultivated the roots of virtue as śrāvakas; and finally, he demonstrates to other sentient beings the wisdom they should practice to gather the roots of goodness.

The Dharma of the Way has but one flavor; yet, according to the inclinations of sentient beings, the roots of virtue they cultivate, and the dwellings, palaces, and abodes where they reside, it appears as a single type to them—or, for those who do not require it, it does not appear at all.

The flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is likewise: it manifests through the cultivation of roots of virtue within the vessels of sentient beings, and thus wisdom-practice appears spontaneously; this is the seventh matter.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when first establishing the celestial palaces Of the Form Realm and the Formless Realm,
Only then do the palaces of the Desire Realm flourish."
Thereafter, it becomes the earth, the dwelling place of the people, all classes of living beings, the nāgas, and the gandharvas.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise: from the beginning, he is naturally so.
Cultivating boundless practices, such is the dignified demeanor of a Bodhisattva;
thereafter, as a serene treasure, they are established through causes and conditions;
next, having attained mastery, they extend their grace to all sentient beings.
When the various drops of rain have fallen, there is neither blue nor yellow;
the water enters the earth, and from this condition various things arise.
Following the nature of that earth, trees, mountains, and groves grow.
That water is not manifold; it is named according to the seeds grown therein.
The Guides abide in the Truths; their wisdom is entirely perfected and holy.
Their compassion and insight are like space, as they maintain mastery over skillful means.
As for the most supreme Dharma, one enters this offering;
wisdom is free from all defilements, and its body has no fixed abode.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like when a calamity of water arises and remains suspended in space; within this trichiliocosm, there appear lotus flowers named Jewel of Accomplished Virtue, which arise spontaneously in various forms, completely covering the transformations of the water calamity and universally illuminating the world.

If these lotuses should emerge spontaneously, when the Great Honored Son of Heaven and the Śuddhāvāsa devas behold these flowers, they will immediately know that in this kalpa there shall arise a certain number of Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“There is a natural wind named Manifest Brilliance that arises and circulates; it brings to completion the palaces and dwellings of the devas of the form realm.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Pure Radiance, which is peaceful, pure, and clean; by means of it, the palaces and dwellings of the devas who course in the desire realm are established.”

Furthermore, there is a wind named "Single Class" (*ekajātīya*), which does not cause destruction, yet establishes the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*mahācakravāḍa*) and the Diamond Mountains (*vajraparvata*).
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Most Honored" (*viśiṣṭa*), which blows to establish Sumeru, the King of Mountains.

Furthermore, there is a wind named Dīrghasthita which blows and brings forth the seven great kings of mountains: first, Gṛdhrakūṭa; second, Gijjhakūṭa; third, Vāhana; fourth, Udayagiri; fifth, Pāriyātra; sixth, Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda; and seventh, Gandhamādana and Himavat.
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Well-Established" (Susthita) that establishes the great earth.
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Adorned and Pure" (Vyūhaśuddha) that establishes the palaces and dwellings of the various gods who frequent the earth—the devas, nāgas, and gandharvas.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Akṣayamati, which establishes the three thousandfold world system and causes all the depths of the oceans to flow.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Ālokagarbha, which establishes the wish-fulfilling jewels throughout all worlds.
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Firm Root" that blows to bring the trees of clothing to fruition.
In this way, O worthy one,
that great rain becomes of a single flavor.
Furthermore, that water is devoid of conceptual thought; it attains the natural order of all phenomena and enables sentient beings to discern the roots of virtue.
Just as these winds use various winds to discern and understand the trichiliocosm.

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has embraced all roots of virtue, accomplished all dharmas, and accumulated unsurpassed, infinite wisdom; as the foremost of the world, he ensures that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed."

The boundless majesty and radiant light were brilliantly manifest, universally illuminating the world and pervading it everywhere; all who beheld this light turned their whole hearts toward the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this Great Sage is free from all obstructions, and the various bodhisattvas each thought to themselves:
"The reason the Tathāgata has now arisen and manifested himself to transform these bodhisattvas is that he has therefore appeared in this world."

He analytically expounds the Buddha-lineage and the pure, stainless, equanimous wisdom; he radiates this light, which is the light of the path of untainted wisdom gathered from the contemplations of the Tathāgatas, named "Universal Illumination," thereby causing the realization of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom of the Dharma-realm and the lineage of perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is a light called "Dhāraṇī"; for this reason, the power of the Tathāgata is unshakable, and as he brings it forth and manifests it, none can surpass him.
There is a path-light called "Transcendence"; for this reason, the wisdom of all Tathāgatas is fearless, and as they bring it forth and manifest it, none can equal it.
There is a light of the Way named "All-Pervading Penetration"; therefore, all Tathāgatas gather and assemble the wisdom of all penetrations, and there is none that does not follow this teaching.

There is a light of the Way named "Destroying Arrogance"; therefore, all Tathāgatas cause the various śrāvakas to see the root of their merits, so that these are not in vain, are without deficiency, and lead to non-attachment.

There is a light of wisdom named Universal Virtue; if any sentient beings behold the Buddha, they are all caused to turn toward inexhaustible merit and wisdom, and their bodies are likewise transformed.

There is a light of wisdom named "Far-reaching and Intermediate"; by means of this profound and wondrous knowledge, the Tathāgata takes refuge in and unites with the Three Jewels of the Ultimate Path, ensuring they are never severed.

There is a light of wisdom named "Adorned with Various Kinds of Purifying Ornaments," by which the Tathāgata is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; having gathered and integrated them all in complete perfection, he brings joy to all people.

There is a light of wisdom named Peerless; by means of this, the Tathāgata traverses the scriptural canons, making them all identical to the realm of space. Within the Buddha-field, his lifespan is immeasurable, reaching to infinity.
Thus it is, O virtuous one!

The Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is of a single flavor; the field of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is free from conceptualization, manifesting the dharmas for attaining the Way of the bodhisattvas and preaching the sūtras according to the faculties of sentient beings.
“The wisdom of the Tathāgata is entirely uniform; the radiance of the Noble Path is equal and without distinction. For this reason, the Tathāgata has arisen and appeared in the world.
O Son of the Buddha!

Observe how this Tathāgata, having attained the single flavor of liberation, manifests through differentiation immeasurable and inconceivable pure virtues, causing all classes of sentient beings to behold and know them; all these are established by the Great Sage.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the Tathāgata to manifest the Dharma without establishing anything.
If one were to encourage and establish even a single person in the unexcelled state, that would constitute the Tathāgata manifesting his fundamental roots of virtue in concert with them.
It is impossible for anyone to fully comprehend the virtues of the Tathāgata or to attain his wisdom through mere conceptualization.

The noble intent of the Tathāgata transcends all dharmas; therefore, he analyzes and manifests them for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to enter into this meaning and to clearly understand the Dharma, never growing weary or satisfied.
The Tathāgata is without conceptualization and without thought; he has no attainment and harbors no expectations; he performs no actions and does nothing that is not done.
He is without an agent and comes from nowhere, yet he manifests and appears—these are the eight matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a lotus flower emerges, so does a Buddha arise;
those devas who rejoice have surely seen Buddhas of the past."
Beholding where the waters lie, the palaces appear clear and bright;
this present world shall not endure much longer, for each shall possess their own realm.
The Buddha’s true and excellent radiance is the primary auspicious sign of this.
The thoughts of the Bodhisattva awaken to and penetrate all things without exception.
His wisdom and consciousness are pure; his body is fresh, clean, and free from defilement.
With the ten powers, he delivers all wriggling creatures and contemplates the practice of all Buddha-dharmas.
Clearly understanding all that exists in the world, and the immeasurable karmas therein created—
yet remaining upon the ground of causes, with the ground resting upon the surface of water,
all situated within empty space— this is called the Great Palace.
Just as bipeds and quadrupeds all rely upon and look up to [their leaders], so it is with the Honored One among Men; having attained realization, he is the Dharma King.
For the sake of all sentient beings without exception, he is the one they honor and depend upon.
All who see or hear him revere and serve him together.
He has destroyed the dust of craving and desire; he is the refuge for the karma of all living beings, reaching upward as far as the Brahma-heaven and extending even to the boundless limits.
For whose sake do you act as a sentient being, desiring to bring peace to the common people?
You should not let your light be obscured by delusion while seeking wisdom;
by providing a metaphor where none exists, the Most Victorious One has thus been seen.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like the four winds standing in space, which sustain the element of water. What are these four?
The abiding wind, the rising wind, the governing wind, and the pervasive firm wind—these are the four.
They sustain the waters of space, and the earth rests upon the water, neither moving nor shaking; this is what is called the power of the earth.
Water rests upon the wind; the wind stands upon space; space has no place of abiding. It is for this reason that the trichiliocosm has its location.
Thus it is, O worthy one!

If one were to conceive of and assemble the manifestation of the Tathāgata appearing in the world, with the unimpeded brilliance of wisdom, there would then be four assemblies of infinite fields of wisdom, which uphold the roots of virtue of all sentient beings.

What are these four? First, the field of wisdom that accords with and gladdens the multitudes at the proper time; second, the field of wisdom that establishes the causes and conditions of all dharmas; third, the field of wisdom governed by the protection of the roots of all virtues, which is fully endowed with all karmic activities; fourth, the field of wisdom that dwells in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) while observing [all things].
These are the four fields of wisdom, by means of which one nurtures all sentient beings.
That which is great kindness is to deliver and liberate all sentient beings;
that which is great compassion is to maintain the lion’s roar.

By being able to establish this great kindness and great compassion, one discerns the various thoughts and inclinations of sentient beings, abides in skillful means, and establishes acts of loving-kindness; this is the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s gracious care.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata is one whose unimpeded, noble, and penetrating clarity abides nowhere; this is the ninth dharma.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the realm of empty space Is without any limit,"
Perceiving both the material and the immaterial, its embrace is immeasurable.
Throughout the eight directions, above and below, all embodied beings within the Buddha-fields and throughout the three realms without exception— this is the realm of empty space.
Such are the bodies of all the Victors; they manifest everywhere, observing the realms of phenomena and the locus of existence and non-existence.
The sublime body of the Great Sage is such that no one can see it at all.
If one beholds the various Guides, one receives transformation and edification according to the Vinaya.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is as if the trichiliocosm were vast and boundless, and the classes of sentient beings therein possessed manifold modes of conduct; yet if there were skillful means that did not depart from empty space—whether in the water, or on the land, or among the *puṇḍarīka* lotuses—they would perform their respective expedient functions in incalculable numbers."
Or they may be within the palaces of the various devas, such as the palace of Maheśvara;
or they may be in space, exercising their mastery through the void.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
If the Tathāgata were to appear and gather [beings], all sentient beings who see him would look up to him with reverence.

Should any come to behold him, they would leap for joy and, according to their desire, abide in the power of awakening, continue the practice of the prohibitions and precepts, delight in great deeds, and become worthy sages who transcend the world.

With sovereign supernormal powers and bodiless wisdom, they expound the gate of noble penetration that is free from obstruction; practicing these deeds, they manifest and proclaim them with mastery, never failing in the retribution of their actions. Their discourse is radiant and brilliant, guiding and benefiting all dharmas; relying upon this great transformation, they forget nothing.
This is called the manifestation of the Tathāgata Saṃgraha; all sentient beings look up to him with reverence. This is the dharma of the ten powers.
Such, O Son of the Buddha, is it!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, manifests and reveals the Dharma through his presence and teaching; it is that toward which one should turn, immeasurable, free from negligence, and devoid of frivolity.
Whatever arises within their mind, intellect, and consciousness returns to the bodiless state, being naturally like space;
they understand that sentient beings are likewise natural, reckoning neither self nor "mine," and are without boundaries or depths.
All Buddha-lands are in fact no lands at all; all lands are utterly empty, returning to non-retrogression without interruption.

In the future, when there is no longer any joy or delight, the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata will be without partiality, returning to non-duality; for all phenomena—whether with form or formless, conditioned or unconditioned—are equal.

If one thoroughly understands all sentient beings and cultivates the practice of the Great Way with self-mastery—this being that which was encouraged and assisted by those of antiquity—one will then be able to fully possess this marvelous and sublime state.
This, O Son of the Buddha,
is the class of those with limitless eloquence.
As for this "class," they embrace and gather together the Great Way manifested by the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings rely upon the Buddha-fields;
all are due to the realm of empty space, and thus they accord with and follow the teachings of the Dharma."
Whether in the water or on level ground, or within the palaces of the devas,
ghosts, spirits, and nāga kings, they all rely upon and look up to him.
Emptiness has no such thought: "What am I creating now?
What have I already lost?
For whom do I manifest this purpose?"
Thus is the Supreme among Men; his body manifests the ease of all conditions, and throughout the ten directions, he performs various deeds.
Delighting himself in the precepts and prohibitions, this Sage of vast karma delivers the world.
With the clarity of supernormal wisdom, for whose benefit and profit do you act?
You demonstrate the pure and white Dharma in accordance with reality; realizing that no self exists at all, you never give rise to conceptual thoughts.
"For whose benefit and for what purpose?
[Thus ends] the first fascicle of the *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
[The second fascicle of the *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha begins.]

“What is it, O Son of the Buddha, that the assembly of bodhisattvas beholds the Tathāgata as being without limit? Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
If a bodhisattva should draw near to the Tathāgata, they thereby take refuge in the Way.
Why is this? One who has nothing to see is the one who sees the Tathāgata.
To see the Tathāgata is to see the single Dharma-body;
with this single Dharma-body, if one directs a single heart of compassion toward a single person, it then reaches all sentient beings, providing sustenance and care to many.

Just as the realm of empty space encompasses all things and penetrates everywhere—reaching all that is with form or without form, with shape or without shape, with location or without location—it neither goes nor comes, and thus possesses no body;
because it has no body, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
The Buddha-body is thus: it universally enters all classes of sentient beings, pervading all phenomena and all buddha-lands without exception; yet it neither goes anywhere nor comes from anywhere.
Why is this? It is because he is without a body.
The body of the Tathāgata manifests only because he desires to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
This, O Son of the Buddha, is the bodhisattva’s entry into the foremost gate; turning toward and manifesting this is what is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha:

For example, space is without color, without visibility, and without form or category, such that it cannot be seen; yet, through conceptual differentiation, one knows the various classes of sentient beings. That which it encompasses is vast, universal, and far-reaching, without any compression, and space itself is devoid of thought or perception.

Thus, when one perceives the body of the Tathāgata universally illuminating the world and performing the work of deliverance, it does not come because of distinct demerits or merits, nor does it go anywhere; it is without obstruction and cannot be apprehended.
Why is this so? Because the light of the Great Sage eliminates all eighty types of perversions; this is the second gateway of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Because they give rise to restlessness, their majestic radiant flames are extinguished;
yet they appear fully to all sentient beings, increasing or diminishing various causes and conditions.
Just as space has no form or color, so too is the Tathāgata."
By means of the single, equal Dharma-body, he rescues and liberates all classes of sentient beings.
As the Most Victorious One has just appeared, he transforms all who are in darkness;
gradually observing the true meaning, they flourish and encounter the Buddha-way.
His morality is exceedingly vast and wide, illuminating the three thousandfold world system;
he delivers beings from the perils of birth and death, his mind entirely free from conceptual thought.
The Honored One among Men is without equal, yet he manifests both increase and decrease.
If there are those who instruct me, may I attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
May all sentient beings know that they should draw near to the Sage among Men,
just as a great Brahmin dwells within his own pure and luminous palace.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
When the light of the sun shines upon Jambudvīpa, all classes of sentient beings receive boundless grace and depend upon it for their livelihood; its radiance is immeasurable."

It is just as flowing water emerging from mountains and rivers provides for the growth of the hundred grains and the materials for clothing; even those places that are deep, dark, and obscure likewise depend upon it.
The wriggling and crawling creatures, as well as oxen, horses, mules, and donkeys, also rely upon it.
Whatever one desires to read or speak of—whether mountain valleys, trees, or various medicinal herbs—all likewise depend upon it.
They completely resolve all disputes and empty delusions;
all classes of beings who roam in the void rely upon them;
and rivers, streams, bathing pools, springs, and flowing waters likewise depend upon them.

The lotus blossoms and unfolds throughout the commanderies, districts, counties, prefectures, and great kingdoms, all of which receive its light; they gaze upon it from one place to another, beholding its various forms and colors.
As it wanders through the fields and among the grasses and sprouts, those on dry land and the species within the waters alike look up toward it.
Each cultivates their own livelihood and whatever they undertake, they are able to bring to completion. Why is this?
The light of the sun’s palace shines immeasurably, and its benefit to sentient beings through the Way and its Virtue is like that of the sun.

If sentient beings behold the body of the Tathāgata or hear his voice, they will attain immeasurable and incalculable conditions through skillful means; by relying upon these, they shall find peace, turn away from evil and proceed toward good, and through the dharmas of merit, eliminate folly and ignorance, extinguish all darkness, and cause the wisdom of the Path to flourish with sublime radiance.
That which is Great Benevolence universally protects all sentient beings;
that which is Great Compassion rescues and liberates the masses.

It takes refuge in all dharmas and nurtures the accomplishment of the power of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. It plants the seeds of pure faith, just as turbid water is brought to clarity.

What is perceived is not in vain; the retribution of cause and effect is never lost. Whether in the realm of form or the formless realm, all matters of birth and death are fully seen and observed. Without causing any harm, the radiant light of the wisdom of the Way causes all sentient beings not to lose their roots of virtue.

As a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is the leader of the multitude, one is like a lotus flower; through the expedient means of the causal conditions of all practices of exhortation and giving, one acts as the most supreme.
Why is this so? Because the site of the noble ones is boundless and bottomless.
Just as the Tathāgata radiates immeasurable rays of wisdom-light, the infinite field of the noble ones is likewise so; this is the third gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the palace of the sun Shines upon all of Jambudvīpa,
Hanging its light in the void, Dispelling darkness without obstruction."
Fundamentally non-existent and without location, yet from the ground arise lotus flowers;
the multitude rely upon them across various lands.
So too is it with the Supreme Sun: all sentient beings depend upon and look up to him.
The various devas and the people of the world, having skillfully cultivated the roots of virtue and subdued the infinite [afflictions], have attained the radiance of the Dharma;
they have come to see the Sage among men and thereby accomplished the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the palace of that single sun, which first illuminates the great stone King Sumeru; next, it illuminates all other great mountains; then it illuminates the Black Mountains; and finally, it illuminates the ridges, mounds, hills, and the various places upon the earth—this Jambudvīpa where people dwell."
The radiance follows the terrain; the light of the solar palace has no conceptual thought, saying, "I shall first illuminate the King of Jewel Mountains.

Furthermore, the sun's manifestation of brilliance is without distinction—whether the ground at a particular location is high or low, it is not the solar radiance that possesses such variation—and thus it does not conceive of priority or sequence.

If the Tathāgata is thus, dwelling equally within the immeasurable, loyal, and upright Dharma-realm at the sublime site of enlightenment, he then emits undiminished radiance, illuminating all things universally with this wisdom-light.

Previously, when the Great Sovereign Śailendra Sumeru King first encountered the light, it was said that he was being led toward the great bodhisattvas, who manifested for him through the light of the Dharma to instruct and deliver him; subsequently, the wisdom yearned for by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas was revealed, so that sentient beings might resolve their minds and establish the roots of virtue. Only then were those of unwholesome factions transformed, and gradually all common folk who had long dwelt in false views were made to receive the light of the Tathāgata.

Having already received the light, they immediately obtain the prediction of enlightenment; in a future age, they shall encounter the Tathāgata Sun-Wisdom Radiance, which causes them to be free from discursive thought and to fulfill all roots of virtue, attaining the brilliance of wisdom according to their vows—this is the fourth gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the radiance of the sun Is never separated from all formed things,
And likewise reaches the hosts of devas, So too do they all find reliance in it."
Just as all the great rivers bring benefit to all people, so too does the Light Abiding One; all sentient beings look up to him with reverence.
Those who are devoid of profound faith do not behold the Buddha’s sun-like radiance.
What is the Buddha’s special distinction, that these beings likewise rely upon his grace?
If there are those who hear his name, they encounter supreme radiance;
by this condition, they gradually attain progress until they reach the path of Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the palace of the sun: those born blind do not see its majestic radiance.
Although they lack eyes and do not know day from night, they nevertheless rely on that light to carry out their livelihood and obtain the necessities of food and drink."
In this way, sentient beings have lost their original purity; seeing the Buddha, they do not believe in the light of the Tathāgata’s infinite path and thus are called those born blind.
Although they do not behold the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, even so, they shall continue to receive the illumination of the Great Sage’s sun.
In this manner, subtle, vast, and brilliant supernormal powers radiate light upon his physical form.
To manifest auspicious responses for the sake of eliminating the conduct of craving, desire, and worldly toil in the future, this constitutes the fifth gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when the sun shines upon the world, those born blind cannot see it;
though they do not distinguish day from night, they continue to receive its radiant light."
"Sentient beings have lost their original purity and do not believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
yet the Buddha’s compassionate grace is vast and great, and they shall continue to receive deliverance.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
It is like the construction of the lunar palace, which manifests four unprecedented qualities.
What are these four?
It illuminates all dark recesses; it remains ever-greatly luminous among the multitude of stars; [it waxes and wanes]; and [it traverses the sky].
Fourth, those who have lost the Way are shown the proper places; they travel throughout the world with a capacity for universal acceptance;
having beheld the moonlight, sentient beings look up to them in reverence;
and wherever they establish themselves or travel, they do so without harboring any doubt. These are the four.

In this way, the body of the Tathāgata possesses four things that are difficult to reach, which have never existed since antiquity; its manifestations are unattainable and are not seen by ordinary persons.
What are these four?
They universally manifest all that is learned and unlearned;
regarding the vows of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they manifest them according to the inclinations and faith of others;
and as for limited circumstances and the duration of their lifespans, they manifest the increase of what has been diminished.
The Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment neither increases nor decreases; it fully reveals all Buddha-worlds and the various classes of sentient beings and their mental activities.

According to their capacity for faith and joy—whether they are fit vessels for the Way or by what light they are moved—they are seen to revere and honor him among all species of living beings, and as they behold the Buddha-body, they all receive his radiant illumination.
Furthermore, the body of the Tathāgata is free from conceptualization, whereby he is able to attain a mind of non-attachment; this is the sixth gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The radiance of the moon shines forth, Its divine aura surrounding Mount Sumeru.”
The light reaches even the various mountains, and then arrives at the hills and banks;
next it illuminates the high ground, and then reaches the level plains;
gradually it shines upon all the lower elevations and every piece of land.
Abiding in tranquility, light first illuminates the bodies of all bodhisattvas;
thereafter it radiates brilliance upon the conduct of pratyekabuddhas, and then it shines upon those with mastery;
next, it illuminates those in training and those beyond training.
Thus they illuminate all beings without exception; in the Buddha-way, there is no conceptual thought.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the Great Brahmā named Trisahasra, who manifests his body throughout the three-thousandfold world system, pervading it entirely without dividing his body."
Whatever species of living beings have physical form, the Tathāgata appears before each according to their appearance and color, such that none fail to see his image.

The Tathāgata, the Most True One, is likewise: he never divides his body nor possesses multiple forms, yet throughout all worlds, he manifests himself in accordance with the dispositions, physical forms, and inclinations of sentient beings. The body and mind of the Great Sage are likewise free from conceptual thought; this is the seventh gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The Brahmā named Trisāhasra Manifests his own form everywhere;
Among all beings, each regards him as supreme, And there is none who does not behold his sovereign power.”
Furthermore, this Brahmā does not divide his essence;
the Teacher of all dharmas likewise possesses such mastery.
The Buddha-body manifests universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
That image is immeasurable, yet its substance is not differentiated;
every person thinks to themselves:
"It is now present before me."
They all beheld the features of the Buddha’s face and heard the Dharma he preached.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a great physician-king who knows all medicines, distinguishing their quality—superior or inferior—and their respective classifications. He is thoroughly proficient in all treatises, scriptures, and incantations; yet there are certain medicinal herbs throughout Jambudvīpa that people do not recognize and deem useless."

The physician’s fundamental virtue, as well as the power of his medical incantations, manifested for the sake of the multitude; upon seeing this physician, all their illnesses were cured and they all attained peace and security.
Furthermore, this physician did not achieve his present standing through the exertion of physical strength, but thought to himself:
"These people are about to lose their protection. After my passing, will they not be left orphaned and destitute? I should surely employ skillful means to manifest myself for them."

He gathers various medicines to anoint his own body; having combined these medicines through the power of his own arts, he manifests the appearance of reaching the end of his life—yet his body does not decay, nor wither, nor crumble. He moves about, comes and goes, sits, rises, and performs walking meditation, all as magical transformations. He employs medicine and therapy to cure the illnesses of sentient beings; those who hear or see his voice also attain peace and security, remaining unchanged from beginning to end.

The Tathāgata is likewise the unsurpassed King of Physicians; he thoroughly understands how to treat the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings. Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, he has prepared medicines, universally returning to the Perfection of Universal Wisdom (*sarvajñatā-pāramitā*) and skillfully learning the arts and medicinal dharmas of expedient means (*upāya*). All of these were established during his past lives as a bodhisattva, as he practiced wisdom, skillful means, incantations, and medicinal foods—maintaining their majestic power until the limits of the future.
Thus, throughout infinite realms of sentient beings, he brings forth protection and salvation, healing the various ailments of all living creatures.
This, then, is to be without body and without worldly activity.

His body is pure; as soon as all sentient beings behold it, their afflictions of desire and exhaustion are entirely healed and cured. Even those who lack faith continue to find peace. Thus, the various works of the Buddha are never interrupted; this is the eighth gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as if there were a physician who had studied all medical arts,
anyone who beheld this teacher would have all their ailments completely eliminated."
Just as when a person is afflicted by illness and distress, one brings medicine to treat them;
having already applied it to one’s own body, one manifests all manner of dignified conduct.
So too is the Honored One among Men: a King of Physicians of immeasurable scope.
Manifesting noble wisdom and having well-mastered the art of healing,
he reveals his venerable and holy body through the practices of his past lives;
thus all people behold him, and their disease of desire is eliminated without remainder.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!

It is as if within the great ocean there were a vast treasury of lapis lazuli jewels called 'Equal Manifestation of All Radiance. Should anyone behold the brilliance of this great jewel, or should they encounter it, their physical form and facial features would all transform to resemble that lapis lazuli treasury."
If people behold the color of this great precious gem, their eyes immediately become pure and they universally attain peace and security;
even the majestic light of the great gem’s palace shines everywhere, and all living beings, receiving its radiance, shall forever be free from affliction.

It is like a great precious jewel named "Peace for the Multitudes" (Anzhong); in whatever year it remains, when it releases rain, all sentient beings immediately attain peace and security, and all calamities are brought to rest.
The radiance of the Tathāgata is likewise so: he is a great treasure, the infinite treasury of wisdom where all blessings converge.
If sentient beings encounter the light of the Tathāgata’s holy wisdom, they shall all attain a uniform state and ascend to the precious image of the path of true reality;
if they behold the Tathāgata, they shall obtain the five eyes.

Encountering the light of the Great Sage, all who are destitute shall obtain the treasure of the Dharma, thereby attaining infinite and abundant wealth, even unto the peace of the Tathāgata Anuruddha.
O Son of the Buddha!

Behold the majestic countenance of Perfect Enlightenment; though there is nothing being spoken, it universally transforms and benefits all, guiding and instructing the multitudes. This is the ninth gate of entry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as one who possesses no rare jewels goes to the deep sea to seek treasure,
and brings forth all manner of luminous pearls, whose radiance shines everywhere."
If a person encounters this jewel, they shall immediately attain spontaneity;
those who behold it with their eyes will instantly obtain the pure eye.
This supreme treasure is likewise: it radiates the light of wisdom.
If a person encounters this radiance, they will attain the countenance of a Buddha;
if they contemplate the Most Victorious One, they will immediately obtain the five eyes,
cast off all dust and darkness, and abide in the stage of the Buddha-way.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

There is a great precious jewel named King of the Treasury of All Pure Recollections. The merit and majestic power of this great precious jewel are not the result of the aggregation of ten or a thousand [lesser jewels]."
Furthermore, wherever that great jewel is placed, the sentient beings in that place shall be universally free from all diseases and afflictions;
should the multitude of people form aspirations and vows directed toward the mani-jewel, it shall cause them all to be fulfilled, and they shall obtain everything according to their wishes.
Furthermore, that precious jewel does not illuminate those who lack the roots of virtue.
The King of Jewels, the Treasury of All Pure Recollections, refers to the Tathāgata, who brings joy to all categories of sentient beings.

Regarding the samādhi of manifesting the body as taught by the Truly Realized and Perfectly Awakened One: he praises and extols the assembly of śrāvakas, so that all sentient beings within birth and death may, amidst the five sufferings, attain a most extraordinary transcendence and cross over from beginning to end.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
The body of the Tathāgata has neither beginning nor end.

For all sentient beings throughout all worlds who have cultivated merit in past lives, their minds become single-pointed and free from distraction; they abide in right mindfulness, purify all their practices, and apply themselves with diligence toward the goal, thereby fully attaining and perfecting all dharma-vows before the Honored One, the Tathāgata.

For those whose offenses are grave and who lack the roots of virtue, such that they cannot perceive the radiance of the Tathāgata, he establishes them so that they may receive his transformative exhortation and be shown their own roots of virtue; this is the tenth gateway of entry.

Acting as a bodhisattva, one proceeds toward true and perfect awakening; entering into proximity with the Tathāgata, one reaches the state of immeasurable mental intention, which pervades all ten directions universally, such that one's practice is without obstruction.
Furthermore, as for the Dharma-realm, one contemplates all realms without abiding in their fundamental limit.
Moreover, the Tathāgata neither arises nor ceases; he is equal throughout the three periods of time and is without any object of thought regarding any conceptualization.

To guide and benefit all sentient beings to the ultimate limit of the future mind, one enters this path so that nothing remains; filling all Buddha-worlds, one becomes fully endowed with the Dharma-body, wherein all Tathāgatas are entirely one pure unity.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a wish-fulfilling gem Can grant all desires,
So too shall those who have a request Obtain exactly what they aspire to."
Those who possess no merit do not see this treasure;
yet regarding this most honored and wondrous pearl, they harbor no thought of stinginess.
Abiding in such a state, they grant all wishes through their generous giving.
If one perceives that there is a place to travel, all that is willed shall be fully accomplished.
Those who harbor hearts of malevolence and peril shall not see the Buddha;
yet the Tathāgata harbors no thoughts of stinginess, nor does he possess greed or envy.
The Buddha addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "What is it, Son of the Buddha,
that is called a bodhisattva following the voice of the Tathāgata, traveling equally throughout all realms to proclaim the sound of perfect enlightenment?"

With immeasurable varieties of resonance and speech, he expounds the Dharma according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, so that each member of the assembly attains what they find pleasing.

He manifests transformations according to their aspirations and intentions; following what the mind conceives, he enters at any time, never losing his samādhi—neither ending nor perishing, neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, when one examines this, it is like calling out to an echo; there is entirely no master and no self, for it is due to the accumulated actions of the merit and demerit of sentient beings.

When one deviates from the profound and subtle, there arises a destination; being remote and difficult to cross, impurity arises, and by discriminating within the dharma-realm, one thus follows [samsara] without interruption.
Because they do not abandon or destroy phenomena, they are without anger or malice, without sinking, and are ultimate;
because they abide in the object of focus, they have neither a master nor a non-master, and there is neither teaching nor non-teaching.
This is what it means to follow the resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice. Why is this so?

It is like when the world encounters a great catastrophe, whereupon there spontaneously arise four great sounds; through these one comes to know the Dharma as being without a master, and thus there is no karma of craving.
What are these four?
When the calamities of the world arise, a great voice spontaneously issues forth:
"Listen, O worthy ones!
"The first dhyāna is peace.
As for the first dhyāna, it is free from the afflictions of craving and aversion; having transcended the realm of desire and attained transcendence, one reaches spontaneity.
Thereupon, when sentient beings heard this sound, they accomplished the first dhyāna, transcended the realm of desire, and were immediately reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Having just attained the Dharma, he heard two voices say:
"O worthy ones, listen!
The second dhyāna is peaceful and secure; it is free from conceptual formations, transcends the Brahma heavens, and brings about mastery."

At that time, when sentient beings hear these two sounds, they practice the second dhyāna; being without perception and without volitional activity, their interior becomes tranquil and their minds are unattached, thereby accomplishing the second dhyāna and immediately attaining rebirth in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Having attained the Dharma, he heard these three sounds:
"O worthy ones, listen! The third dhyāna is most peaceful;
it is free from the desire for joy, the mind is tranquil and settled, and internally there is no conceptualization."
"The third dhyāna practitioner, following the instructions of the Noble Ones, transcends the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that time, when sentient beings heard these three sounds, they transcended the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Having been born in this heaven and attained this Dharma, one hears these four sounds:
"O worthy ones, listen! The fourth dhyāna is tranquil;

it eliminates suffering and removes ease, sorrow and joy; being neither painful nor pleasant, it is pure and complete. This is the fourth dhyāna, which transcends the Heaven of the Fruit of Departure."
At that time, sentient beings, hearing these four sounds, abandoned the heavens of the Fruit Devas and were reborn in the pure heavens that are difficult to reach.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
When the world undergoes calamitous transformations, one hears these four great sounds and thereby attains the Great Canon.

"The sounds of nature have no presiding master; the virtue of the Great Sage is lofty and immeasurable, and his natural voice is subtle, exquisite, and supple, spreading far and resonating to the ends of the earth."
Thus, it is without a master and without anything created; there is neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate, neither elevation nor depression.
If there is one who wishes to attain the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there will spontaneously arise the four great sounds and the four great teachings.
What are the four?
First, a voice proclaimed:
"Those who do not cultivate merit shall all suffer from affliction."

The three realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as the conceiving of a self and a person, the claim that "this is mine," and the greedy attachment to all things one possesses—these too are suffering.

If one plants roots of virtue, one will be born among gods or humans, receive the teachings of the sages and saints, abandon the hardships of birth in the eight states of no leisure, and practice the ten wholesome deeds; thus all calamities shall be removed, and one will always encounter the Buddha-dharma.
The two voices spoke, saying:
"Virtuous ones, listen!
All phenomena are suffering; they burn with fierce heat, mutually oppressing one another."
When one contemplates the manifold afflictions of thought, the body is seen as impermanent.
The law of separation is formless and quiescent; by not being intent on gain and honor, the flames of passion do not blaze, and one immediately departs from all hardships.

At that time, having heard these words, the multitude of people upheld and practiced them; gradually becoming more diligent, they attained the Śrāvaka vehicle and crossed to the other shore by means of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
A third voice proclaimed:
"Beyond the Arhats, there is a subtle and exquisite vehicle of delight called the Pratyekabuddha; one attains self-awakening without a teacher."
