Thereupon, having heard these sounds, those people increased their faith and joy slightly and attained the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
Four voices then proclaimed:

"Beyond the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is the practice of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, which encompasses rafts and steers great ships to ferry others to the other shore; they do not sever the mind of the Way, and their deliverance is infinite as they protect and sustain beings from beginning to end."
Because sentient beings suffer from weariness and aversion, there appear Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

As for the Mahāyāna, it is the most honored vehicle, the most extraordinary vehicle, the vehicle upon which all sentient beings rely and look up to, and the vehicle of the supreme, true, and correct path for those who believe and delight in it.

Having heard this sound, those whose faculties were clear and penetrating, who had planted roots of virtue in the past, and who were established by the majestic spiritual power and holy intent of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—having been made such that their will and nature became vast, expansive, and luminous—they attained mastery in sincerity and thus gave rise to the aspiration for the Way.
The sound proclaimed:
"All Tathāgatas have no body and no mind; they neither manifest nor transform, yet cause sentient beings to obtain peace and security."
"Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first causal matter by which bodhisattvas may attain compliance with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the voice of the four immeasurables is universally proclaimed throughout the world,
so the realm of sentient beings is pure, having originally emerged from the boundless void;
thus there are the four wisdoms, tranquil and secure in dhyāna."
When the multitude hears this resonance, they immediately abandon the realm of desire.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise: pervading the entire dharma-realm, for the sake of sentient beings, he proclaims immeasurable sounds.
Whoever attains this seal transcends the marks of the conditioned and dwells securely in the resonance of sound, never again harboring thoughts of doubt.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
For example, just as sound arises from an echo between the crags and rocks of a deep mountain, so it is with the world:
when one records these worldly conventions, there is neither speech nor body; yet when one sees something, one calls out, and in response, sound arises.
All sounds and speech arise from conditions encountered by the ear; if one examines them with truthfulness, they are forever devoid of conceptual thought.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
The voice of the Tathāgata has no verbal instruction, nor does it have any location.

When sentient beings conceive thoughts of the Way, their intentions arise due to causes and conditions; yet when one investigates the principle of sound, there is no resonance, and it cannot be apprehended. This, O Son of the Buddha, is what it means.
"Second, by taking phenomena as their object, the bodhisattvas attain compliance with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as in the midst of deep mountains, An echo arises due to causes and conditions,"
Responding to whatever is called out by the multitude, he immediately returns every sound.
The Buddha transforms and guides all sentient beings, using his voice to bring them to enlightenment;
though he employs words and speech, he has never harbored a single thought of doubt.
The resonance of the Ten Powers is free from attachment throughout the Dharma-realm;
distinguishing and guiding sentient beings, it disciplines and transforms the source of their faculties.
Toward all subtle and minute beings, it causes them to feel joy and satisfaction.
Those who possess the ten powers do not harbor deluded thoughts in their seeking.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

Just as when a great thunderclap produces a sound, it is called "the True Dharma of the Gods"; even if the gods wander about in negligence, at that very moment the thunder of the Dharma resounds through the void.

"All sensual desires ultimately lead to impermanence; they are but momentary afflictions, delusions, and deceptions. One who is foolishly habituated to them fails to realize this and lacks heedfulness; do not exert yourself in pursuit of them."
"If you indulge yourselves in self-indulgence, you shall surely fall into the evil realms; do not allow yourselves to become deluded.

Upon hearing these words of instruction, the heedless devas were immediately filled with sorrow and distress. Each of them renounced the pleasures of desire and went to the palace of the Heavenly King, where they delighted in the inexhaustible teachings of the Heavenly King and reverently practiced the Dharma.

Furthermore, observe that the sound of this Dharma-thunder can be spontaneous and without distinction; it arises as a causal condition for the multitudes of devas and humans, produced for the sake of establishing all sentient beings.

The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it cannot be grasped, yet it resonates with the sound of the Great Dharma according to the conduct of beings. It is a voice free from craving and karma, free from negligence, and a voice of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. It proclaims to the entire dharma-realm, reaching everywhere without exception and pervading all sentient beings. According to their inclinations, it exhorts and transforms them so that they find joy; it guides them through the three vehicles, each leading them to their proper place. This is the practice of Bodhisattvas who possess immeasurable and sovereign wisdom, causing all to enter into the inconceivable.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses no wealth of wisdom nor any fixed abode, yet he entices and proclaims it to all.

Having heard this sound, incalculable multitudes of sentient beings diligently practice in accordance with these roots of virtue; some seek the vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, while others resolve upon the unsurpassed, ultimate Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, the sound of the Buddha-way pervades all things; it is without attachment and beyond verbal expression. This is the third way in which bodhisattvas attain conformity with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Even if the heavens were to become negligent, Thunder would naturally roar,
Revealing the nature of all phenomena, Causing one to delight in the meaning of the Path."
Then, from within the void of space, the sound of proclaiming the Dharma resounds;
when the devas hear this voice, they immediately reform and cease their wild galloping.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise: like a thunderclap, he spreads the rain of the Dharma.
Flowing forth to the ten directions, it guides and benefits all sentient beings;
possessing supreme speech, it transforms others.
Having heard this resonance, the masses shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a celestial son named Īśvara, also known as Subhadra, whom all look toward with expectation; then hundreds of thousands of varieties of jade maidens gather before him, playing drums, lutes, and harps, singing in harmony with the strings, their rhythms manifold, as they perform various exquisite melodies upon their instruments.

If the Tathāgata is thus, he employs a single voice that accords with the minds of sentient beings; according to their original aspirations, natures, and inclinations, and based on what they find pleasing, he manifests various teachings through his immeasurable practices so that each may attain understanding according to their respective faiths. This is the fourth way in which bodhisattvas attain conformity with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when Māra indulges in self-will, He produces celestial music,
with the beauty of jade maidens, Whose rhythms and measures harmonize with one another."
With single-minded devotion they sing praises, their voices in unison producing wondrous melodies;
they possess hundreds of thousands of millions of diverse and novel sounds.
Such are those possessed of the Ten Powers: they constantly manifest a single sound that proclaims all teachings.
Thus, through skillful means and expedient power, his voice and breath bring joy to all living beings.
As the common people follow with faith and delight, if they hear his verbal teachings, their afflictions are severed upon hearing them; yet his voice remains free from conceptual thought.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the Great Brahmā dwelling in his celestial palace; in the mere instant of forming a thought, the sound of his command and admonition spreads far beyond and reaches the assembly, causing all the Brahmās and the sons of the Brahma-body to reverently receive his decree."
Thus it is, O worthy one!

The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, utters the unsurpassed and subtle Buddha-voice, universally addressing the entire assembly. While remaining silent within, his voice reaches the ten directions, delivering all sentient beings and leading them to the site of enlightenment.
The Tathāgata’s compassion is equal toward all, and he is without parsimony regarding sentient beings.

Those whose faculties are not pure, who are not tranquil, and who do not take delight in seeing or hearing the transformation of the Dharma—all of them gather together at the site of enlightenment, each thinking in their own mind:
"Now, the Tathāgata is preaching the sound of the Dharma for me alone."

"Furthermore, the voice of the Tathāgata has no object of control, yet it establishes that which is appropriate for conversion; this is the fifth way in which bodhisattvas attain conformity with the voice of the Tathāgata."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Even if one attains the exalted station And the seat of Brahmā,
Yet with but a single word of instruction, One may delight the heart of Brahmā."
The resonance of that Brahmā does not escape outward;
he fully knows all minds, as well as the intentions of the assembled multitude.
Endowed with the virtues of the Ten Powers, he sits pure upon the Buddha’s seat.
Then he emits a single sound that pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
it does not conflict with the various assemblies, nor does he harbor greed or parsimony.
Those who lack firm faith do not hear the resonance of the Buddha’s voice.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!

It is like water, which is fundamentally equal and of a single taste throughout, yet undergoes various transformations according to the vessels it enters; thus one distinguishes and knows that each taste is distinct."

If the Dharma-teaching is thus, and the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Way is of a single flavor—namely, the flavor of liberation—yet the minds and dispositions of sentient beings differ such that they perceive what is spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One as being diverse, the Tathāgata’s voice remains free from conceptualization; this is the sixth way in which bodhisattvas attain compliance with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when one measures all waters, All rain is naturally of equal taste and pure,
Free from impurity and possessing the eight kinds of sweetness;”
O Sons of the Buddha, in this way, they clearly understand the voices of sentient beings;
if their resolve and mindfulness are of a single flavor, they attain the spontaneous path of the Buddhas.
Through the encounter with causes and conditions, they manifest various distinctions according to each stage.
The vessels are each distinct, causing the water within them to remain forever different;
so too, among all the various classes of beings, the actions of sentient beings differ,
and according to their minds they hear the Buddha’s voice, which is why what they hear is not the same.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

Just as when the great dragon king Anavatapta intends to send rain, dark clouds spread everywhere over Jambudvīpa, and only then does he let fall the rain, causing the hundred grains, various medicinal herbs, trees, bamboos, reeds, thickets, and forests to all grow lush and flourish, their flowers and fruits becoming abundant."
The sources and currents of all rivers issue forth from the body of the Dragon King Avimukta, causing countless things and immeasurable species to attain nourishment and benefit.
It is thus, O virtuous one!

The Tathāgata pervades all worlds without exception; with abundant great compassion, he pours down the rain of the great Dharma of ambrosia to gladden sentient beings, causing their merit to flourish and fully perfecting all vehicles throughout the ten directions.

The voice of the Tathāgata does not emerge from within, nor does it come from without; yet thus immeasurable and incalculable people, and all classes of sentient beings, bear it upon their heads and look up to it. This is the seventh way in which bodhisattvas attain conformity with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the many flowing waters Circulate throughout Jambudvīpa,
Reaching everywhere without exception, Universally moistening the great earth."
Mountains, hills, grasses, and various trees, as well as the five grains, all depend upon water for their growth;
yet one who observes this water finds no conceptual thought regarding its source.
The World-Honored One is likewise: proclaiming all realms of phenomena, he spreads the rain of the True Dharma, filling the multitude of sentient beings.
He nurtures hundreds of thousands of virtues and eradicates all worldly afflictions.
Having fully understood the Buddha’s words, one does not run about in external pursuits.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the great Dragon King Manasvin: when he intends to raise a great rain, he first gathers and accumulates clouds that pervade all the celestial palaces, reaching everywhere without exception; yet he may not release even a single drop of rain, but observes whether the people’s agricultural work is fully prepared before he finally lets it fall.
Why is this? It is because he does not wish to afflict sentient beings.

He thinks to himself that if the great dragon were to descend slowly and deliberately for seven days, releasing only fine droplets, they would pervade the fields and cause much growth and flourishing.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is the Great Dharma King; he raises the heavy canopy of the Dharma to transform and enlighten sentient beings.

Whatever he speaks, he rains down the flavor of ambrosia for those of pure and virtuous nature, and only thereafter does he unfold the infinite transformation of the Way, raining down the moisture of the Dharma to expound the profound and esoteric scriptures, so as not to cause sentient beings to harbor any fear.

To proclaim the flavor of unsurpassed, universal wisdom, filling many with it and enabling them to achieve its realization—this is the eighth way in which a bodhisattva accords with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as there is a noble dragon named Mānasa,
who rains for seven full days, moistening the earth gently so that nothing is harmed."
This is why the Naga has come: desiring to fulfill the karma of sentient beings, he then manifests compassion and brings down a rain of peace and security.
Relying on the multitude through his Ten Powers, he gathers like clouds to spread the shade of the Dharma.
In order to transform sentient beings, he reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
According to the capacity of each person, he proclaims the profound sound of the Dharma.
Those who hear this proclamation without fear or alarm shall enter the wisdom of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the great ocean where there is a great dragon king named Mahā-vyūha-viśuddha (Great Adornment-Purity), who in a single thought-moment can produce ten kinds of rain; countless hundreds of thousands of species are all thoroughly moistened by it.
The rain has no conceptual thought, nor does that dragon king have any differing thoughts; the rain occurs spontaneously, yet it causes hundreds of thousands of varieties to be distinct."
Thus it is, O worthy one!

When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wishes to manifest the rain of the Dharma-sound, in the mere instant of forming that thought, he discerns ten dharmas and understands their ultimate destination. He proclaims the radiance of the Dharma and emits a hundred kinds of sounds; or again, he fully elucidates the eighty-four thousand practices of sentient beings, manifests eighty-four thousand resonances of entry, and extends to the teachings of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vocal expressions, gladdening the hearts of infinite sentient beings.
The Way of the Dao and the sounds of the Dharma are likewise free from conceptualization, yet they completely dissolve all fundamental roots.

The Dharma of the Tathāgata—whether through infinite compassion or its various transformations—is thus virtuous, wondrous, pure, and magnificent; this is the ninth way in which bodhisattvas attain compliance with the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when the Great Pure One, The eldest son of the Dragon King,
First causes the clouds to gather, And only then lets fall the rain."
The Buddha-way is spontaneous, yet its Lord has those whom he delivers;
from his mouth issue ten kinds of sounds, twenty, or even a hundred, or again a hundred thousand. The bounty of the Dharma is without limit.
The Honored One has nothing that is not fully expressed, nor does he destroy the Dharma-realm.
The Dragon King of Self-Mastery, the most honored among all dragons,
lets his cooling rain fall everywhere, reaching throughout the four quarters of the world.
Moistening all that has form, it lets fall rains of various kinds;
yet the waters within the ocean possess no such diversity.
So too is the World-Honored One: the teaching of the Way is of a single, uniform flavor.
The minds of practitioners differ, and thus what they attain is likewise not the same.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
When the Great Dragon King of the Ocean wishes to manifest the infinite, moving transformations, he invariably brings peace to sentient beings, causing them to feel joy and exultation."

It rained upon the four continents, pervading the entire earth and reaching upward as far as the palaces of the Sovereign Clear and Pure Heaven (*Īśāna-svarga*), where clouds were spread to provide shelter and shade for various classes of beings.

Furthermore, these multitudes of clouds simultaneously manifested such forms, diverse and distinct: some were the color of purple gold, some yellow, some the color of lapis lazuli, some white silver, some crystal, some red pearls, some with the luster of agate, some with the luster of musaragalva, and some with the luster of śūta.
Thus, they are covered by a vast, composite cloud that extends universally across the four quarters and the four continents.
Furthermore, although the water itself is without distinction, the clouds and mists manifest in various different forms.

Having manifested lightning, he let forth the great sound of thunder and rained down according to the desires and inclinations of all living beings: sometimes producing the sounds of celestial maidens singing and playing music; sometimes the sounds of heavenly lutes, harps, and various instruments played in harmony with flutes; sometimes the musical sounds of various nāga queens, or the musical sounds of gandharva queens, or the musical sounds of asura couples; sometimes the sounds produced by the land, or the sounds of musical performances like the thundering of the ocean; sometimes the lowing sounds of the king of deer, or the musical sounds of the invincible bird (*amogha*), or various kinds of ten-thousandfold dance performances.
The vast canopy of great clouds that covered it appeared in such a form and color that the seasons were greatly gladdened, and naturally, dragon-winds blew everywhere.

As these winds emerged, the clouds and mists remained serene; first they released fine drizzles, and thereafter they scattered a great rain—reaching upward to the Sovereign and Pure Heaven and spreading downward across the earth, the void, and the celestial palaces, reaching everywhere without exception—and it rained upon the great ocean without causing any destruction.

Furthermore, in the realm of the Īśvara devas who dwell in pleasure, he rained down music and dance performed by celestial maidens named "Joy"; in the realm of the Asaṃtuṣṭa-māna devas, he rained down various wish-fulfilling jewels; in the Tuṣita heaven, he rained down pearl necklaces and ornaments; in the Yāma heaven, he rained down various kinds of flowers; in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, he rained down soft, renowned incense; in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings, he rained down fine garments; in Uttarakuru, he rained down exquisite flowers; in the palace of the Great Naga King, he rained down "Transcending Light" red-luminous pearls; and for the Asuras, he rained down weapons called "Destroyer of Enemies."
In this manner, throughout the four directions and the realms of the four continents, the rain poured down upon all the celestial palaces in such abundance that it was beyond calculation.
The Great Dragon King of the Ocean felt no stinginess and harbored no envy.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha! The roots of virtue planted by sentient beings are each distinct and not uniform; accordingly, they naturally transform into rain that is uniquely differentiated.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, as the Great Dharma King by means of unsurpassed wisdom, constantly manifests the joy of the Dharma for his own delight; yet, in profound stillness, he universally disseminates it throughout the Dharma-realm, with the cloud-banks of his Dharma-body pervading everywhere without exception.

He manifests according to what sentient beings believe and delight in: sometimes he proclaims and clearly demonstrates the body of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for sentient beings to raise the rain of Dharma; he manifests transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) to release the rain from the clouds of Dharma; he manifests established bodies to bring down the rain of Dharma; he manifests bodies of physical form with various kinds of rain; he manifests bodies of merit to spread the cloud-rain; or again, he manifests the cloud-rain of the wisdom-body (jñānakāya); or again, he follows worldly convention to manifest a body endowed with the ten powers (daśabala), or manifests the four fearlessnesses (catur-vaiśāradya)—spontaneously revealed and without deficiency—or manifests the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without a physical form. This is the great Sage’s Dharma-body (dharmakāya), whose pervasive rain covers the entire world.
According to the inclinations and faiths of sentient beings regarding their voices, he manifests radiant light for them to eliminate all defilements and turbidity.

This light is called "Equal Radiance," or "Immeasurable Light," or "Pervading the World," or "The Secret and Profound Treasury Established by the Buddha," or "Light Illuminating the World," or "Inexhaustible Practice Entering the Gate of Dhāraṇī," or "Unconfused Intention," or "Peerless Mind," or "The Range of Wandering Steps," or the light is also named "Delighting All Aspirations."
In this manner, through the thunderous resonance heard from the rain of Dharma, one attains true awakening and clearly realizes the Buddha-way.

If one hears the thunder of equality with purity, one immediately masters the seal of detachment from defilement—the natural sounds of the thunder of samādhis: the samādhi of sovereign mastery over all dharmas, the vajra-field samādhi, the Sumeru-banner samādhi, the sun-stationed-light samādhi, the great ocean-seal samādhi, the samādhi that accords with the minds of the multitudes, the inexhaustible-resonance liberation-free-from-anger samādhi, the samādhi of being without desire for worldly pleasures, and the samādhi of constant compassion without fail. Should these sounds be raised, they cause each person to hear this sound of the Buddha-Dharma.

“This is the body of the Tathāgata, which distills ambrosia and brings forth countless clouds and rains of Dharma sounds; the teachings it proclaims are heard by those who travel without peer, delighting all sentient beings—this is the inconceivable gateway to the omniscience of perfect enlightenment.”

To gladden the hearts of all sentient beings so that they may all attain their proper time, this is called the "Dharma-assembly of Realizing Vast Wisdom and Accomplishing the Immaculate Expedient Means of the Past. It is characterized by great kindness and great compassion, ultimate freedom from negligence, and the flourishing of the Way’s transformation; this is that which is to be followed.
All Bodhisattvas first settle their bodies and minds, and only then do they manifest the rain of the Great Dharma. It is thus, O Son of the Buddha!

Just as these forms and images manifest the rain of the Great Dharma, the rain of compassion, and the inconceivable rain, so too does the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, through the awakening of equality, guide all sentient beings and transform their bodies and minds, pouring forth the inexhaustible, infinite nectar that cannot be exhausted.

"When he arrives at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he shall proclaim for all bodhisattvas a great rain of Dharma called 'The Non-Destruction of the Dharma Realm,' which most thoroughly brings about the realization of the stage of *avaivartika*;
and another great rain of Dharma called 'The Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata, Delighted in by Bodhisattvas,' which brings to fulfillment the state of being a bodhisattva in his final birth;
and there is a great rain of Dharma called 'Adorned Purity,' which causes all living beings universally to be free from transgression and never to abandon the bodhisattva path."
"In the stage of the Tathāgata, there is a great rain of Dharma called 'Adorned Path, Self-Ornamented, and Attaining the Endurance of Dharma,' wherein all Bodhisattvas gather as a treasury of wisdom.
There is a bodhisattva practice called 'Skillful Transformation,' which elucidates the rain of Dharma without any interruption;
it is the practice of the Bodhisattva named 'Door of Non-Arrogance,' who enters the profound gate and practices without weariness or sloth."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-rain that causes those who have first resolved upon the Bodhisattva path to follow the unsurpassed way; this is called the practice of the Tathāgata.
With great kindness and great compassion, he intends to rescue all living beings;
he raises up the rain of Dharma to transform those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Practicing within the sphere of faith and aspiration, he manifests for the multitude the locus of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Or, transcending existence to attain the fruit of liberation, he is named "One Who Enters the Universal Limit" regarding all views and phenomena; thereupon he spreads the rain of Dharma and opens the Śrāvaka vehicle, such that sentient beings believe and rejoice.

Using the sword of noble penetration to sever all stains of worldly affliction, possessing the wisdom-sword while spreading the rain of Dharma, one is named "Delighting in the Extinction of All Harm. For those with various wrong views who cannot comprehend, one accumulates the roots of virtue and rains down the sounds of all dharmas; this is called the ten dharmas that fully manifest the rain of Dharma, which completely fills and pervades all things.
According to their faith and inclination, so that they may attain liberation, the Tathāgata then manifests the great rain of Dharma, pervading the entire dharma-realm and reaching everywhere.

The Great Sage has never been stingy with the Dharma; rather, according to the matured conduct of sentient beings, he manifests the rain of Dharma through various roots of diligence. This, O Son of the Buddha, is how it is.
The Tenth Matter of the Practices of All Bodhisattvas:
"Just as clouds and mists gather, and winds arise from the four quarters,
surpassing the seasonal rains and the flowing waters."
The Bodhisattva has analytically explained the root of virtue for all beings;
therefore, in the present world, he establishes this trichiliocosm.
Such is the nature of those possessed of the Ten Powers: they have skillfully cultivated wisdom as their wind.
Through causes and conditions, he pours down the rain of Dharma; his will and nature are exceedingly pure.
Observing that sentient beings are without equal, he encourages and assists them with purity;
these are what are called the Ten Powers, by which the Guide brings about transformation and enlightenment.
Above in the void of space, clouds gather and rain falls;
none are able to bear it, nor can they hold back the falling water.
Only when the world encounters a calamity and transformation is it able to endure and receive it.
The words of his speech are true and unattached; his physical realm is vast and universal.
Such are the Ten Powers, spontaneously non-existent.
Whatever the Great Sage has spoken are the words of the Dharma-realm.
Yet he rains down the Dharma to transform and teach, its moistening power beyond limit;
none are able to sustain it, save those whose will is pure in the Dharma.
Never has such a thought arisen: regarding the origins of the past and the future.
Furthermore, there is nothing created, and forever nothing encountered.
Just as clouds and mist bring forth rain within the void of space, so too are all phenomena merely provisional names; they arise spontaneously and without transformation.
The Ten-Powered Ones are thus: the rain of Dharma has no locus;
there is neither one who comes, nor has any ever been seen to go.
Exhausting the majestic spiritual power of all Bodhisattvas, they bring forth these practices.
Having realized that phenomena are illusory transformations, one attains the world and lets fall the rain.
When sentient beings have no more wandering, there is then no triple world;
it is like a natural shade from which drops of water descend accordingly.

Only the Honored One possesses sovereign mastery; the name of the teaching throughout the three thousandfold world-system was established by him with complete freedom—this is fundamentally the fruit of his merit.
May peaceful rains fall like this, pervading the Buddha-lands without exception.
His mindfulness and his measure are such that no one can calculate them.
Toward all sentient beings, he is the Honored One of all worlds;
thus he contemplates and rains down the treasure of the Way as if it were held in the palm of his hand.
In tranquil extinction one should be serene; naturally, one attains understanding and penetration.
Furthermore, one cuts off all other matters and the various hindrances that arise.
Casting aside these manifold blemishes, one ever increases the precious practice of the Way.
He presides over the three thousandfold world system, fully understanding all things.
He knows the source of the Ten Powers, extinguishing the dust and toil of worldly desires;
his contemplation is spontaneous, and his myriad virtues are immeasurable.
Furthermore, having severed and cast away all false views,
and having discerned the nature and conduct of the will, one becomes rich with the most supreme treasure.
This single flavor of the True Dharma is like rain falling from the sky.
The rain that falls has no limit, yet each scattered drop has its own place.
Furthermore, when one calculates that water, there is no notion of what is appropriate or inappropriate;
the multitude harbors joy, just as all phenomena arise from causes.
Furthermore, as for that Dharma: it does not arise as one, nor as many;
its fundamental flavor is equal and uniform, and it is free from the notions of what is appropriate or inappropriate.
"Reaching to the very limits of the boundless,
even the Buddhas and the assembly of sages shall uphold such a semblance-dharma as this.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"By means of ten qualities of renown, the voice of the Tathāgata enters into the limitless.
What are these ten?
It enters into space and is thus limitless;..."
They reach universally into all phenomena and all realms without limit;
they enter the realm of non-remainder, discerning and clearly understanding the realms of sentient beings without limit;
they enter into all things, gladdening the hearts of the masses and understanding the destinies of both transgression and merit without limit.
He enters into the realms of causes, conditions, retributions, and sentient beings, removing the fetters of worldly toil with immeasurable wisdom;
he enters into the ultimate, tranquil, and serene sound of non-arising with immeasurable depth;
he transforms others according to their inclinations, entering into the mind of liberation with immeasurable scope.
They enter the three realms by following the flavor of liberation, boundless and without limit;
they abide in the bottomless and attain the state of no-realm, entering the practice of wisdom without limit;
they select the essentials of all dharmas, and within the realm of the Buddhas, they do not turn back, remaining without limit.
Entering into the Tathāgata, one accords with the Dharma without effort and without limit.
Thus it is, O Bodhisattva Viśuddhanetra!
For the sake of immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings, you cause the resonance of their speech to flow forth as the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By means of the ten virtuous qualities, One enters the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom;
Reaching all phenomena, The sphere of its scope is without limit."
The Great Way is likewise thus: towering and beyond the reach of thought, it brings compassion to many, so that all are granted deliverance.
It discerns the limits of birth and death; the myriad classes of beings are inexhaustible.
Transforming and eliminating all sins and merits, he gladdens the mind and brings about liberation.
He causes one not to seek karmic retribution; his wisdom of the Way is boundless and bottomless.
Having thoroughly understood the Buddha’s voice, he suddenly enters into profound stillness.
The Sūtra on the Arising and Manifestation of the Tathāgata, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Second.
The Sūtra on the Arising and Manifestation of the Tathāgata, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "What do you mean, Son of the Buddha? How do the bodhisattvas enter and roam within the mental activities and thoughts of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"

The Tathāgata does not have anything for the mind to think of, does not differentiate names, and does not cognize through consciousness; it is because the Tathāgata is without mind that he is able to enter and roam within immeasurable thoughts.
Just as all things are constructed by relying upon empty space, and because of that space they are brought to completion, yet empty space itself is entirely without attachment—
so it is, O worthy one!
If one seeks the Way and relies upon wisdom, all mundane and supramundane matters arise and become manifest through the noble wisdom of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is without attachment; this is the foremost gateway of causal conditions into which a bodhisattva enters while dwelling in the recollection of the Tathāgata’s conduct.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as within the void of space, All forms are received;
Though one relies upon them with attachment, Yet there is no conceptualization of 'space'."
The wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata is thus free from all attachment;
it universally rescues all beings, yet conceives no notions of self or person.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the dharma-realm is not separate from all that is practiced and traversed by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
furthermore, that dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases—such is the Great Way.

The Tathāgata’s wisdom gathers together the wisdom of both the mundane and the supramundane; he discerns and understands the skillful means created by thought, and his wisdom neither increases nor decreases—this is the second.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the stages of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
and the great beings who are bodhisattvas, all arise from empty space."
The Great Sage is likewise thus: possessing the boundless wisdom that understands emptiness, his mind is equanimous without increase or decrease, and he provides salvation without partiality.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the great ocean, which connects with the four great continents and eight billion lands; wherever the terrain extends, reaching to its very boundaries, water can be obtained everywhere, surfacing spontaneously, yet that great ocean has no such thought.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise so: it reaches the minds and hearts of all sentient beings, pervading them all without exception.
According to what the various masses of people intend and contemplate, he attains the pure Dharma-gates appropriate for them and thereby causes the people of the world to obtain spontaneous wisdom.

Furthermore, the wisdom expounded by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is entirely impartial; according to their respective dispositions and natures, he treats them with extraordinary means. His virtue and Way transcend the world—this is the third.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Just as the four great oceans are entirely interconnected with eight billion realms."
Water reaches everywhere and wells up spontaneously,
yet the ocean has no conceptual thought;
such is the wisdom of the Tathāgata, reaching the hearts of all sentient beings, with nothing that his wisdom does not penetrate.
Following what the multitudes desire, he guides and instructs them,
leading them to pure clarity and enabling them to attain natural luminosity;
all that he expounds is entirely impartial, for the Tathāgata is free from conceptual thought.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like the great ocean, which naturally possesses four great wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) that gather and accumulate immeasurable virtues.
As for the reason these wish-fulfilling jewels come to be, it is not because dragons or spirits possess virtue that these great jewels are produced; rather, they arise spontaneously."

All rare and precious things owe their existence to the grace of the great ocean; it gives birth to all treasures, and among the common people, there are none who do not rely upon it for their sustenance.
What are these four? First is named the Equal Gathering of All Treasures; second is the Inexhaustible Sound; third is the Refuge; and fourth is the Equal Gathering of All Words.

Furthermore, it is reckoned that this great wish-fulfilling jewel cannot have its radiance produced by any ordinary beings—neither asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, nor the various nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and other blood-dwelling creatures who inhabit the waters.
Why is this so? Because the jewels are firmly held within the treasuries of the Sea Kings and Dragon Kings.
Furthermore, the various maṇi-jewels in that great ocean have four corners; they stand individually in the palaces of the Dragon Kings of the four directions.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: his moral virtue is brilliantly radiant, and he possesses the four great jewels of infinite wisdom. By means of these four great jewels of wisdom, he exhorts, transforms, and guides all sentient beings—whether they be those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas. Through the conditions of these jewels of wisdom, there are none who are not brought to salvation.
What are these four? They are:

the wisdom of skillful means that promotes the joy of the Dharma to the point of non-reliance; the wisdom of the treasury of Dharma-jewels—both conditioned and unconditioned, numbered and unnumbered; the wisdom that manifests at the appropriate time without destroying the nature of all dharma-realms; and the wisdom that attains transcendence over both timely and untimely disturbances. These are the four.

Then, further employing the wisdom of these four great elements to seek the Tathāgatagarbha and enter the treasury of the Way, one does not share in the defilements of sentient beings; while remaining in the world, one attains the wisdom of a bodhisattva, causing all bodhisattvas to travel through the four quarters to practice what they should, establishing them firmly in unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, and setting them upon the stage of non-retrogression—this is the fourth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The noble meaning of the four treasures leads to the attainment of the peaceful and wondrous treasury;
thus, within the great ocean, all manner of jewels are produced spontaneously."
That wish-fulfilling great jewel is never apart from its pure excellence;
though it manifests distinctions in the four directions, wherever it resides there is radiance.
So too are the Tathāgata’s four kinds of wisdom—immeasurable and beyond limit.
Abiding securely in the sublime and lofty state, he opens the path for those in the five realms of existence.
This is the boundless, ultimate wisdom; it is free from divergent thoughts.
He observes all throughout the ten directions, and there is nothing among his teachings that is not fully realized.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
Within that great ocean, there further appears a wish-fulfilling jewel of the four great elements, its majestic power sublime and its radiance infinite."
The radiance of this wish-fulfilling jewel’s merit dispels the waters accumulated in the great ocean, causing those waters not to overflow; thus, the great ocean neither increases nor decreases.
For this reason, the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel causes the great ocean to remain perpetually filled.
What are the four? They are:

the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of the Sun’s Radiant Treasury, the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of the Lion’s Gait, the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of Shining Radiance, and the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of Ultimate Exhaustion of Remainder. These are the four great jewels.
If this great ocean were devoid of such a wish-fulfilling jewel, its waters would overflow, and the four great continents would be submerged in a vast, surging expanse.

However, when the wish-fulfilling jewel known as the Sun-Luminous Treasury (Sūryaprabhā-garbha) is present, it transforms the waters of the great ocean through two means: its light illuminates them, subdues and evaporates the water, and causes its color to change, forming an image like milk;
the light from the wish-fulfilling jewel known as the Lion’s Gait (Siṃhavikrānta) then transforms the color of the milk, making it appear like a lump of clarified butter (sarpis).

When the radiant brilliance of the wish-fulfilling jewel shines upon it, the image of Sū is removed; just as at the time of the kalpa-ending conflagration, when the flames blaze so fiercely that they consume both heaven and earth, the light of the great wish-fulfilling jewel shines upon the vast ocean until nothing remains, suddenly extinguishing it entirely, such that its destination is unknown.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, illuminates all things with the four kinds of wisdom.
By means of this luminous illumination, he leads all bodhisattvas until they attain the samādhi of a Tathāgata.

What are these four? To eliminate all transgressions by means of the river of Dharma; to bring the exhaustion of affection and craving to completion so as to achieve the transformation of the Path; to illuminate the world entirely with the light of wisdom; and for the Tathāgata’s insight to be neither darkness nor light, being the equanimity of the Sage—these are the four great insights of the Tathāgata.

For the sake of all bodhisattvas, they endure various terrors and plant the roots of inconceivable merit; yet as for those among the various classes of devas, humans, and asuras who dwell in turbid worlds, they are unable to withstand their afflictions and immeasurable sufferings.

If one encounters the tranquil realm of the Tathāgata, illuminated by the light of wisdom, one subdues all attachments and establishes oneself in samādhi; if one hears the verses of the Dharma, one dries up the ocean of birth and death.

Having encountered the Tathāgata’s wisdom of transformation and being deeply devoted to the Samādhi of Joy, they thereby give rise to the subtle sounds of the Great Sage’s supernormal powers and wondrous conduct. With great wisdom illuminating the world, they dissolve all defilements; through the practice of the divine feet, they achieve self-establishment, acting as a great light for the world to open the path for those who are blind and obscured, such that there is neither darkness nor ignorance.

By being able to receive this noble wisdom of the Tathāgata, one can subdue the false wisdom of the world; though there is no meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the stage of a Great Man, one eliminates all wealth, occupations, and bribery, and having nothing pertaining to the body, one attains the wisdom of this Great Way.

If one lacks these four kinds of wisdom, the path of virtue, and the light of the Tathāgata, it is impossible for the assembly of bodhisattvas to attain the samādhi and right concentration of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; nor can they eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor achieve the four fearlessnesses and the practice of the beginningless limit—these constitute five matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The waters of the sea have no limit, Yet within them are four kinds of treasures:
The one of great power and boundless majesty, And next, the subtle and most honored."
The myriad streams of the four quarters naturally flow into the great ocean, yet the great ocean neither increases nor decreases.
So it is with wisdom seated upon the Dharma-throne: it decisively cuts through all attachments.
Bestowing the Dharma as a vast gift, they rejoice without words.
Abiding securely in the four wisdoms, they serve all the bodhisattvas, the most excellent ones, and the bodhisattvas; they have never experienced any afflictions.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
To use an analogy: from the waters below up to the realms of the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above, all the trichiliocosms are situated within space."

Considering it in this way, all sentient beings within the triple world who possess form do not exist apart from empty space; yet when one contemplates the self as void and finds nothing to grasp, there is no dependence. Being empty and without attachment, one is neither constrained nor oppressed.
Birth and death are likewise so; one observes throughout the ten directions the entirety of empty space, which encompasses all Buddha-worlds, yet there is nothing therein that is grasped.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
The wisdom of all those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle—the wisdom of conditioned practice and the wisdom of unconditioned practice—all rely upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

That which is opened and transformed by the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the Great Way that penetrates and universally enters all things; it is nowhere not pervasive, free from conceptual thought, and without obstruction. It immediately employs sagely wisdom to deliver and guide many; this is the sixth.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"The sublime purpose extends from the lower regions, Arising up to the higher realms—
Throughout all the three thousandfold worlds, Including the desire, form, and formless realms."
Abiding nowhere, yet not abiding in anything; in all realms there is no self, nor does one reckon things as permanent, nor dwell upon their cessation.
Abiding securely in wisdom such as this is the root of all wisdom.
All those in training and those beyond training, as well as those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the many Bodhisattvas of clear realization, who harbor a mind of compassion—
if they were to establish the gateway to the Path, the Buddha’s wisdom would remain supreme.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the great medicinal herb that grows from below and reaches the summit of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, known as 'Rootless.

Moreover, this great medicine has roots that penetrate beneath the earth, extending sixty-eight thousand yojanas past the vajra-sphere, where it stands securely within the water-element, such that no one is able to uproot it."

Its source is distributed throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, where the sprouts of all things gather around the roots and trunks of every tree—growing stems from near the stems, branches from near the branches, nodes from near the nodes, leaves from near the leaves, flowers from near the flowers, and fruits from near the fruits; all the trees, flowers, and fruits in the world arise because of it.
Furthermore, as for the "Great Medicine" (Mahauṣadha), its root transforms the body and the body causes the root to transform;

because these two functions do not give rise to the myriad things, and because it is close to hell—relying on water which is purely yin—it does not undergo transformation despite being there, and thus it cannot arise within the dharmas.
Furthermore, it is the natural law that the roots of medicinal herbs are spread throughout all other regions of the great earth, reaching to the very limits of where such plants grow.

The wisdom of the Tathāgata’s path is likewise: being fundamentally pure, it gives rise to the root of firm resolve through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); the seed of equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) constitutes the ultimate truth; and its subtle penetration of the essential points is unshakable—this is called the "root.
Skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is called the "stem."
Wisdom is the branch;
the dharma-realm is the joint;
the single-minded liberation-gate, samādhi, and right reception, which are indestructible, are the leaves.
The adornment of the awakened mind is its flower;
the full development of the tree-like form is the various supernormal powers and wisdoms;
and the liberation of knowledge and vision is its fruit.
That his eloquence is thoroughly proficient in all deliberations is called "earth.
That the wisdom of the Tathāgata is without root or attachment—
by what cause is it without root or attachment?
To have forever nothing in which to place faith is what is called "thoroughly penetrating"; thus, there is no rooted attachment.
Whatever may arise is entirely without activity;
when bodhisattva practice is severed, it is then without basis, and for this reason, one is called a Tathāgata.
To manifest the conduct of a bodhisattva is what is called being without dependence or attachment.

If a bodhisattva draws near to the source of the Tathāgata’s infinite wisdom, they will not abandon or forsake any sentient beings; because of that root of the Way, they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
To draw near to its stem is to possess firm vigor (*vīrya*).
Because its stem gives rise to branches in succession, it is the Perfection of Diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), which brings about long-term accomplishment;
because the branches produce leaves, it is the training in the prohibitions and precepts (*śīla*), which is tranquil and knows the proper time;
that which is near the flowers refers to the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the manifold roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*).
"Jie" (sections) refers to acting according to the times;

"subsequently producing fruit" refers to thorough mastery, namely the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), reaching a state free from coarse speech, being gentle, harmonious, benevolent, and refined.
Furthermore, its "fruit" consists of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), which constitute the fruit of the Path.
For this reason, the wisdom of the Tathāgata does not arise from two things.
What are these two? They are the great vast valley of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Even if one falls into the mountain torrents, one wanders in the infinite and unconditioned matters of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, one’s disposition does not conform to them, yet there is no fear; one wanders at the source of the three cravings and the three flows, and regarding the wisdom of the Tathāgata, neither does it arise nor does one regress.

If there is anything that arises, one has already attained the nature of the sages and cultivated a mind of equanimity; regarding all bodhisattvas, there is no distinction between self and other. Furthermore, one contemplates the Great Path of Perfect Enlightenment as brilliantly radiant, majestic, and bottomless, taking this as the ultimate truth.

Wisdom neither increases nor decreases, its faculties remain firmly established, and it causes all sentient beings to ultimately attain thorough penetration and clear understanding, yet they have no fixed conviction; this is the seventh matter of the Buddha’s son.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"On the ridges of the Snowy Mountains, there is a medicinal herb named *Amūlaka*.
This medicine possesses great divine power, its majestic radiance being peerless."
Universally nurturing all, the various trees of the forest—
with their roots, trunks, leaves, and branches— the branches do not exist apart from the roots.
The seeds of all Buddhas naturally accomplish the wisdom of the Way;
their virtuous intent is likewise such that they cultivate and practice all-knowledge.
Clearly understanding the practice of the Buddha-way, they reverently proclaim the sacred path.
They cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, and thereby grow in awakening and wisdom.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like the calamities at the end of an eon, when a great fire blazes fiercely, burning the trichiliocosm; all trees, medicinal herbs, and myriad things, even up to the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, and the Great Diamond Mountains, are without exception consumed by the flames."
Suppose someone were to take withered reeds, lush pine needles, and heavy rafters and cast them into a blazing fire; what do you think?
Would there be even a single leaf that would not burn?
He replied, "It cannot but burn; there has never been anyone who could prevent it from burning.
He reported this, saying:
"In this way, one might still be able to prevent fire from burning trees, or place limits upon a great heap of firewood and grass.

Yet, regarding the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom, his threefold penetration, and his divine insight—concerning the number of sentient beings, the extent of lands, the depths of all dharmas, and the infinite kalpas of past, future, and present—it has never happened that there should be anything he does not universally perceive, nor any subtle obstruction that he cannot fully reach."

Why is this so? Because the wisdom of the path of perfect enlightenment is without limit, incalculable, and all-pervading; therefore, he is titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. This is the eighth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“If a kalpa encounters calamity, Heaven and earth are subjected to smelting;
In an instant, everything is scorched to cinders— Men, women, trees, and fruits.”
O Son of the Buddha, reflect and consider this:
even vajras would melt away in these various realms; how much more so withered grass and wood?
As for all that exists upon mountains and hills, how could it possibly escape being burned?
With wisdom firmly established, they are able to discern and know all things:
the classes of sentient beings in the future, the various kalpas and buddha-fields,
and how all Buddhas fully penetrate these matters— thus, they are immeasurable and limitless.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

Just as when the winds of calamity arise, there is a great wind named Destroyer of Light (*Vidyā-vināśana*). It then breaks forth and rises up, destroying the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, and the Vajra mountains; it blows throughout the entire trichiliocosm, scattering and dispersing them until nothing remains."
Furthermore, there is a wind named *nidānasaṃvartanī* (the Covering of Causes and Conditions) that blows across the trichiliocosm, lifting, supporting, and transporting it to other Buddha-fields.

If this *nidānasaṃvartanī* wind were to encounter alone the *svairacārī* (self-indulgent) and *avipraṇāśaprabha* (undestroyed brilliance) winds, it would immediately shatter the immeasurable Buddha-realms of the ten directions.
Thus it is, O virtuous one!

The Tathāgata possesses a boundless great wisdom called "Destroyer of All Dust and Desire," by which perfectly awakened one all the afflictions and hindrances of the assembly of bodhisattvas are blown away and removed.

Next, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable holy realizations called "The Great Empowering Expedient Means of Universal Comprehension," by which he is able to eliminate the afflictions of the fetters of craving and reach the most wondrous site of enlightenment; thereupon, he further transforms and guides newly initiated bodhisattvas and all those whose faculties have not yet matured.

If the Tathāgatas did not collectively employ this great skillful means to establish the Great Bodhimanda, they would cause the countless and incalculable assemblies of bodhisattvas to practice the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The World-Honored One, in accordance with skillful means and expedient methods, causes the bodhisattva mahāsattvas to transcend the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; by virtue of this, they attain mastery and abide nowhere—this is the ninth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“If within a kalpa there should be terror, And the various devas are disordered and ill at ease,
Even the divine enclosures and Mount Sumeru Shall all be utterly destroyed.”
The wind immediately arose, and none were able to restrain it;
immeasurable Buddha-fields were pulverized without remainder.
Yet those who dwell throughout the ten directions, having attained mastery through holy compassion, remain unharmed.
Thus, by means of destruction and shattering, they eliminate the afflictions of all bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there is the wind of the Way; by following and practicing skillful means (upāya), they immediately provide protection and deliverance, bringing peace to the practitioners of the śrāvaka vehicle.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata enters into all things; his noble intelligence is so lofty that there is no realm of beginning and end among all sentient beings to which it does not pervade."
Why is this so? Because it is impossible for anyone who possesses the conceptualization of desire to attain or reach the wisdom of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is entirely free from all marks; his sovereign wisdom wanders in spontaneity, without any obstruction.
It is as if one were to write a single scripture whose volume is as large as the trichiliocosm;
or there may be a great scripture not yet completed, as vast as the ocean of the trichiliocosm, or like Mount Meru, or like Mahāmeru, or like the entire earth.

To state the essentials: it is as if like a thousandfold world-system, or like the realm of the four continents, or like Jambudvīpa, or like the great ocean, like Mount Sumeru, like a great divine palace, like the abodes of the gods of the desire realm, like the gods of the form realm, or like the gods of the formless realm.

Suppose a great scripture were compiled, vast and expansive, as large as the trichiliocosm; yet within this great scroll there is a single mote of dust, and upon each of the various scriptures there is likewise a mote of dust, such that they all completely fill the interior of the great scroll.
At that time, a man appeared spontaneously, intelligent and wise, who entered [the vessel] to test it himself.
Possessing the divine eye, his vision was pure and all-seeing; he observed it with that divine eye:
"Now this scripture scroll is as vast and infinite as this, yet upon it there is but a tiny speck of dust, which brings no benefit whatsoever to sentient beings."
I would rather, by means of my infinite strength and the power of great diligence, tear asunder this scripture and unravel this great scroll, so as to bring benefit to all the common people.

As soon as he had thought this, he immediately exerted the power of infinite vigor and the momentum of diligent effort; thus, according to his wish, he took the great scripture scrolls and distributed them individually to provide for the common people.
Just as there is one sutra scroll, so too is the number of all sutras. It is thus, O worthy one!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, by means of his immeasurable wisdom and incalculable radiance, enters entirely into the mental activities of the ocean-like minds of all sentient beings, and universally understands the aspirations and characters of all living creatures.

The wisdom of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, all-pervading, and inexhaustible; the knowledge of the Perfectly Enlightened One is beyond calculation. As he observes the realms of all sentient beings, he marvels at this unprecedented phenomenon:
"How can these classes of sentient beings be so foolish and deluded as to be unable to discern the holy wisdom of the Tathāgata?"
The World-Honored One entered everywhere and thought to himself:
"I should proclaim and reveal the Great Way so that all bonds of conceptualization may be naturally eliminated.

By the power and majesty of the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the sacred path, he shall cause all clinging thoughts to be abandoned; he shall cause them to understand the meaning of the destination of true and correct wisdom, to attain the concentration of infinite samādhi, and to eloquently expound the Right Path. He shall remove all conceptualizations and instruct them in the wisdom of the unsurpassed Way, transforming all beings within the five realms of existence so that they reach the Infinite. This, O Son of the Buddha, is it!
The tenth matter:

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, exhorts all bodhisattvas to enter the meaning of the Path. In this manner, he delivers countless bodhisattvas and others, causing them to receive the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which transforms their minds and leads them into the Great Way.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Suppose there were a scripture scroll as large as the triple-thousandfold world system,
upon which naturally formed atoms were scattered all over it."
There was a wise man with clear vision who tore up a sutra scroll, divided it into pieces, and distributed them to those in the five realms of existence.
The World-Honored One is likewise; his wisdom is like a great ocean.
Observing the minds and intentions of sentient beings, All of whom are deluded by various conceptualizations,
The Buddha, out of compassion for humanity, Acts to dissolve their manifold thoughts;
The Bodhisattvas look up to him with reverence, Truly discarding attachments in successive order.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
What is meant by a bodhisattva entering and roaming within the realm of the Tathāgata?
In this regard, the wisdom of the bodhisattva enters without obstruction, knowing that all realms are the realm of the Tathāgata."
All the objective realms within all Buddha-lands and the realms of sentient beings are entirely without origin; they are not partitioned, nor are they subject to destruction.
This Dharma-realm has no limit of the aggregates or obscurations.

Furthermore, the "original limit" (pūrvakoṭi) is a limitless boundary—just like space, it has no shores, no boundaries, and yet it is not non-existent; it entirely enters and dwells within the realm of the Tathāgata.
Just as the seeds of sentient beings are immeasurable and have no boundaries, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata; it is likewise immeasurable and without limit.
Why is this? Because the thoughts and inclinations of sentient beings are incalculable, the Tathāgata accordingly transforms and guides them through his immeasurable wisdom.

Just as a dragon king, being honored and possessing sovereign power, gathers immeasurable waters and, at the proper time, releases rain in incalculable drops—neither emerging from within nor from without;
so too is the realm of the Tathāgata: whatever he intends to bring forth is spontaneously accomplished, for he has no one to consult and no teacher.

Just as the water in the great ocean is immeasurable, yet all arises from the thoughts within the mind of the dragon king, so it is with all the infinite, holy, and penetrating practices leading to supreme wisdom that resemble the ocean of Dharma; these are all the vows established by this Bodhisattva in the past when he first resolved his mind, arising through the distinctions of those very practices.
He asked: "What is meant by 'the immeasurable as the great ocean'?
What is meant by 'the infinite ocean of all supernormal knowledges and wisdom'?"
He said: "It is inconceivable; there is much that could be explained, reaching as far as the great ocean.
Now I shall briefly set forth the essentials and explain them in detail. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon them well."

In Jambudvīpa, there are five hundred rivers that flow into the great ocean; in the realm of Aparagoyānī, likewise five hundred rivers flow into the great ocean; in the realm of Pūrvavideha, four thousand rivers flow into the great ocean; and in the realm of Uttarakuru, ten thousand rivers in their entirety flow into the great ocean.
"What do you think?
Would the water that has converged and flowed into the great ocean increase in volume? He replied:
"Very much," he replied.
"The water rained down by the Dragon King Daśaraśmi is more than the flow of all those rivers."

Furthermore, all the waters existing within the four great domains, as well as the rain falling from the Dragon King Ten Rays that enters the great ocean, do not equal the water rained down by the Dragon King Hundred Rays that falls into the sea; the latter is the most abundant.

Furthermore, the great waters rained down by the Dragon Kings of the Ten Lights and the Hundred Lights throughout the four great regions that enter the vast ocean do not equal the water that enters the great ocean from within the body of the Great Roaming Dragon King; the latter is twice as much.

To state the essentials: as the rain from the roar of the dragon king Manasvin is doubled, so too is the rain produced by the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda; and the rain from the dragon kings Amitaprabha, Varuṇa, Mahātejas, and Mahāpraśvāsaka is likewise.
These ten great dragon kings and the King of a Billion Dragons each rained down water beyond measure.

The waters of the great oceans in the four continents, the water rained by the ten dragons, and that of all eighty billion species of dragon kings all returned to the great ocean; yet it was not equal to the water of the eldest son of the Dragon King of the Sea in Jambudvīpa.
The waters of all the great rivers and the torrential rains do not equal the water produced in the palace of the Great Dragon King Daśaraśmi;

even when one considers the waters of all the rivers in the four great continents, the rains from the aforementioned dragon kings, and the water produced in the palaces of the Dragon King Daśaraśmi and the Great Dragon King Śatarasmi, none of these compare to the water produced in the palace of the Great Pure Adornment Dragon King (Mahāvyūha-viśuddha).

To speak briefly, Maṇasvin, Āśani, Nanda, Upananda, Anantaprabha, Mahāmaṇivicitra, and Mahāprabha—all these dragon kings, as well as the water produced from the palaces of the eighty billion dragon kings, are entirely inferior to the water produced from the palace of Sāgara, the Dragon King of the Long Lineage.
In this way, while the waters of all the dragon kings flow into the great ocean, none are equal to the rain produced by the Great Dragon King Sāgara, which is most abundant and indestructible.
This includes the waters of Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru,
as well as those rained down from the palaces of the Ten-Ray Dragon King and the palaces of the Hundred-Ray Dragon King and the Great Lapis Lazuli Dragon King.
As for the rain that falls from the palaces of the Mānasa Dragon King, Vajra-ghoṣa, Nanda, Upananda,
A-pramāṇa-prabha, Su-kumāra Dragon King, Mahā-tejo-dīpta Dragon King, and Mahā-vijṛmbhita Dragon King,
as well as that which issues from the eighty billion species of Dragon Kings— whatever such [rain] there is:
The rain showered by the eldest son of the Naga King of the Four Great Continents and Oceans, and the indestructible rain of the Naga King Sāgara—
though these great masses of rain are all incomparable to the waters produced within the pure lapis lazuli of the Great Naga King Sāgara,
which completely pervade and fill the great ocean; such is the infinity of the waters of the great ocean.

"Furthermore, just as the waters of the ocean are immeasurable, so too are the realms of its precious jewels immeasurable; the realm of sentient beings is likewise limitless, and even when observing their vast bodies, they cannot be calculated."
The waters of the great ocean are immeasurable, and the varieties of its precious gems are likewise limitless.
O Son of the Buddha! What do you think? What is your understanding of this?
"Is the water of that great ocean indeed limitless?
He replied, "It is limitless."

"Just as the virtues of the great ocean cannot be measured, so it is with the Tathāgata; his wisdom is limitless, such that even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or a hundred-millionfold comparison cannot serve as a metaphor for it."
Not relying on mere words, but according to what people understand, the Buddha uses the analogy of the great ocean to illustrate that the Great Way of the Buddha is far more sublime than this.
By means of provisional samādhi, its illumination is boundless; thus, the majesty of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that he has realized is like the great ocean.
Their intention is limitless, continuing without interruption from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment through all the practices for the omniscience of a bodhisattva;
the treasure of the Way is immeasurable, for the dharmas of all the factors of enlightenment and the Three Jewels can never be exhausted.
In exhorting and transforming sentient beings, one should cultivate this contemplation:

whether they are learners or those beyond learning, all those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are seen to be delivered. Through the ultimate truth and a will that abides nowhere, they perceive the immeasurable and dwell in the stage of supreme joy.
From the very beginning, a bodhisattva is able to reach the stage of non-obstruction and transform all other bodhisattvas so that they do not fall back or retreat. Thus, O Son of the Buddha!
the assembly of bodhisattvas is able to roam within the realms of all Buddhas, and is also able to pervade universally all that exists, without limit or measure.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Accumulated are all pure categories, Incalculable and immeasurable;
The sphere of manifold thoughts Is entirely without limit."
The limit of such mastery is that the mind has no bounds;
one should seek this state within all those who possess the ten powers.
Just as a dragon dwells in its abode, never departing from it, so too should one abide.
In accordance with what his mind conceives, he releases a shower of rain drops.
Even if the mind were to come, it could then be brought back;
yet that dragon has no such thought.
"I shall now cause a rain to fall.
All those who possess the Ten Powers are thus:
none have ever come, nor is there any returning; the Able One (Śākyamuni) cannot be apprehended."
Eternally there is nothing produced; how much less could there be any intentional thought?
The Dharma-realm is without limit, like the sands of the Ganges;
its oceans have no boundaries, and so it is with their waters and treasures.
In all the abodes of sentient beings, throughout the entire immeasurable expanse, the water is of a single flavor; all who live therein rely upon it.
If one dwells within this realm, one does not consume any other water through the power of karma.
The Great Sage is likewise thus: his wondrous wisdom is without limit or depth;
the Three Jewels are unimpeded, and the essentials of the Way are incalculable.
Whether those who train or those who do not, and the countless multitudes of people—
Countless multitudes of living beings aspire to the wisdom of the Buddha-way. "What is it,
Son of the Buddha, that is called the unimpeded practice through which a bodhisattva enters and dwells in the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata?"

His deportment and etiquette were just like those of a Tathāgata; he had originally been without birth, and in future ages there would likewise be nothing he created—yet he appeared suddenly through the conditions of the times.
This practice of the Tathāgata neither arises nor ceases; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and it does not enter into the conditioned or the unconditioned.
It is like the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which has no limit, yet is not without limit.
Why is this so? Because there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*) and no body, it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
A Great Sage is thus; he is named Tathāgata because his practice is neither limited nor unlimited, and he dwells within the bodiless and the non-self-existent.

It is like a bird flying through the void of space; though it may fly for hundreds of thousands of years, there is both that which is traversed and that which is not traversed. Whether looking ahead or examining behind, that space has no boundaries.

The conduct of the Tathāgata is likewise: though he may discourse on the infinite for billions of koṭis of kalpas, or praise it as having limits, even if he were to say nothing at all, the conduct of the Tathāgata remains, by its very nature, boundless.

The Tathāgata already abides in unimpeded conduct and yet has no place of abiding; nevertheless, for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests such and such modes of conduct, universally delivering them from all traces of impediment.

Just as the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda) soars through the void, observing the palaces of the nāgas with his pure eyes, he transforms his original form and recognizes those whose end has come; then, spreading his wings and flapping them vigorously, he strikes the waters of the ocean until the waves are churned and the depths are laid bare, seizing and devouring the nāgas along with their wives and consorts.

The Tathāgata is thus: his wisdom is unimpeded, and he abides in bottomless practice. Throughout the entire dharma-realm, he universally observes the faculties of sentient beings—whether they be pure or mature—and according to their past roots and the seeds of various virtues they have planted, he manifests forms by means of the infinite ten powers of a Tathāgata. He enters the ocean of beginning and end, plows through the abyss of birth and death, and guides the multitudes. Being able to act as a suitable vessel, he extracts the masses from the ocean of beginning and end; therein he establishes their resolve, and within the teachings of the Buddha-way, he completely severs all verbal and physical conduct, attaining the state of a Tathāgata who is free from all conceptualization.
Because they are free from conceptualization and their wisdom is unimpeded, they abide in non-abiding.
Just as the light of the sun and moon illuminates the world while they travel alone without companion, they have no fixed station and traverse the path of empty space.
When the people look up, the sun and moon do not think:
"I have something to report, or perhaps I shall return.
So it is with the World-Honored One: he wanders in *nirvāṇa* and enters the pure Dharma without any conceptual thought.

Within the realm of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they manifest and transcend all conditioned activities; they tirelessly deliver the multitudes of beings across the five destinies, attaining unimpeded mastery without relying on any specific faith, and they proclaim the Buddha-work without coming or going.
This, O Son of the Buddha, is how all bodhisattvas enter the course of practice of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; it is neither limited nor unlimited, as they act on behalf of all conditioned phenomena.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The rootless is inexhaustible; Never has there been arising or ceasing.
For one who reckons the rootless, Nowhere is it not visible."
The compassion of all is such as this; their conduct is immeasurable.
That which is without origin is spontaneous, and thus there are no two distinct things.
Just as with these various seeds, the dharma-realm has no fixed location.
Furthermore, it is neither limited nor unlimited; the practice of the Way is likewise so.
The noble realization has no shore or bottom, and that which is discerned is infinite; this, then, is the absence of a body.
Just as a bird might travel through space for billions of kalpas,
with its beginning and end likewise indistinguishable, so too is the realm of emptiness perfectly equal.
For hundreds of thousands of supreme kalpas, one should discourse upon that which is to be practiced.
Just as skillful means lead to fulfillment, one does not lose their virtuous merit.
Like the golden-winged bird soaring in the sky, gazing from afar into the water,
he knows when the dragon’s life shall end, then seizes and devours both the dragon and his queen.
With mastery over the wisdom of the ten powers, he utterly consumes all afflictions;
having skillfully established the roots of myriad virtues, he uproots the source of birth and death.
Like the sun and the moon, he travels through the midst of space.
The common people receive peace and security, yet light remains free from conceptual thought;
so too is the World-Honored One: through the unimpeded Dharma and the assembly, he transforms and guides countless beings without giving rise to any conceptual thoughts.
"What do you mean, Son of the Buddha?
How does a bodhisattva enter the path opened by the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the bodhisattva universally transcends all practices of attachment without hesitation; through the equal flavor of the Dharma, they realize the non-dual entry expounded by the Tathāgata, and thus further enter into the awakening that is without conceptualization, the awakening that is without activity, the awakening that is without location, the awakening that is within the limitless, and the awakening that is without boundary."

Abandoning what is unaccomplished and relying upon the intermediate state, one then contemplates all written characters and sounds as having no locus, and within all spoken words and voices, there is no verbal teaching.
