Having reached the ultimate limit of the conduct of sentient beings and upheld equal enlightenment, their mental dispositions, faculties, and afflictions of desire were all rendered pure; with the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom, they were universally equal toward all things throughout the three periods of time.

It is like the great ocean, which all the people of the world revere and look up to; it encompasses all sentient beings and perceives all those with bodies, and for this reason it is called the "great ocean.

The Way of the Tathāgata is likewise: he beholds the minds and the dispositions to which the multitudes of living beings incline. Although there is that which illuminates, there is no thought of illumination; thus it is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). For this reason, it is called the Way of the Tathāgata.
That which is guided and led forth is itself transformed by that which can guide and lead; thus, although characters are expounded, there is nothing spoken.
Within all sounds, there is nothing proclaimed; though there are verbal teachings, fundamentally there is nothing said.
Even if there is something to rely upon, there is nothing to rely upon.
Furthermore, I shall now explain in general outline how I exhort and transform all classes of sentient beings:
the path of the Tathāgata brings those who are converted to the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment, without limiting it to any particular class of beings.

Just as it is with the name of the Tathāgata, so too is it with the number of bodies abiding, the number of all lands, the number of all things existing throughout the three periods of time, and the number of all abiding bodies; these are likewise thus, without distinction.

Just as it is with the number of the Way and its teachings, the number of all words, the number of the dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas, the number of empty space, the realm of non-obstruction, the realm of verbal instruction as opened up and guided by the practice of all guides, and the limit of nirvāṇa, so too is it with the number of places where the physical forms of sentient beings abide;

the limit of the words of the mouth is likewise thus. Just as it is with the numbers of body and mouth, so too is it with the limit of the number of places where the unobstructed mind abides; they are equal and without difference.
By entering into such countless states of practice, he purifies the three spheres and attains the Way and its Virtue.
For this reason, he governs himself and all sentient beings with equanimity; beholding all things as thus tranquil, he observes them and leads them equally toward the realm of Nirvana.
Having beheld such spontaneity as this, all enter into the state where there is neither spontaneity nor the exhaustion of spontaneity.

Non-arising and non-ceasing are likewise spontaneous; self and non-self are likewise spontaneous; person and non-person are likewise spontaneous; even the Buddha’s absence of conceptualization is likewise spontaneous; the dharmadhātu is spontaneous, and the spontaneity of empty space is itself without spontaneity.

Having fully understood this, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment and reached the wisdom of the True Dharma that leaves nothing remaining; he beheld the Tathāgata’s boundless great compassion and extensively transformed and enlightened all classes of sentient beings.
Just as space contains and receives the world, so too do all directions, customs, aspirations, and natures naturally come to be within the world.
By such analogy, there is no exhaustion, no increase, and nothing that is produced;
that which is produced is likewise tranquil, and even the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment involves no awakening.
Furthermore, as for those marks, they are neither that which is marked nor are they marks themselves, yet they are not manifold.

It is, for example, like a man who creates transformations and metamorphoses people into Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, making them peerless and beyond description; having thus manifested these, he then further proclaims that the sands of the Ganges are all but kalpas.
"What do you think?
By what kind of transformation does that person’s emanation cause [beings] to resolve their minds on awakening and become Tathāgatas?
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"As I understand it, I shall now clarify the meaning:
the number of emanated Tathāgatas is like that of those who are not emanated;
the same applies to the number of emanations themselves."
He replied: "Excellent, excellent! It is truly as you have said.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!"

In a mere instant, all living beings shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment; the number of those who become Bodhisattvas shall likewise be thus, and those who do not achieve it shall likewise be thus, with neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Furthermore, when one examines the Way, it is devoid of marks (*nimitta*).

That which is markless has no realization of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and nothing to be increased or benefited; even if one attains perfect enlightenment, there is nothing to be reached.
These bodhisattvas shall enter into the Tathāgata in this manner and thereby attain perfect enlightenment.
If they wish to awaken to this realization, they should cultivate this awakening:
"The Tathāgata is of a single characteristic and identical in nature; thus, there is no characteristic of difference."
This is called the Samādhi of the Perfect Enlightenment of Wisdom.

Having attained mastery over meditative concentration, he realizes the Dharma-body in its entirety, leaving nothing remaining, and thus transcends the physical existence established by all sentient beings.

Just as when one person attains supreme perfect enlightenment and reaches the gateway of the Way, so too it is for all sentient beings who attain the Buddha-way and reach the Dharma-gate; they are equal and without distinction.

They cause immeasurable people to attain the gateway of perfect enlightenment and to enter, abide, and dwell within the infinite realms of the Tathāgatas' various bodies, which are without limit or bottom.

The realm of sentient beings is incalculable; these bodhisattvas enter the Tathāgata who has attained supreme perfect enlightenment, each attaining it individually, just as sentient beings fundamentally enter the body of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because if one attains universal entry into the gateway of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, then the conduct of one’s body neither arises nor perishes.
Just as one attains this one matter, so it is with all others;
thus does one enter and traverse the entire dharma-realm, neither departing from its locus nor abandoning words.
To have faith in this is to be one who possesses the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because if one can universally enter [this state], one achieves perfect enlightenment and reaches ultimate wisdom; thus, one propagates this profound stillness and proceeds to the Bodhi tree to ascend the lion throne.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva universally understands that his own mind can achieve perfect enlightenment, he enters the Dharma-body.
Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Arhat, does not abandon the fundamental nature of the mind, and thereby attains the Great Way."
As it is with one's own mind, so it is with all others; thus, by guiding and instructing all minds, one should enter this state.
This, O Son of the Buddha! is what it means.

The assembly of bodhisattvas, for the sake of these great sages, uses this inference to enter and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment; it is vast, far-reaching, and all-pervasive, universally entering everything without exception or abandonment. Being free from attachment, they never weary or slacken; being free from fixed convictions, they enter the gateway to the inconceivable dharma-realm.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Already liberated from duality and non-duality, He has clearly realized all phenomena;
Equal to space itself, He universally understands all scriptures."
Having realized that there is no self, this is the liberation from all phenomena;
having discerned the noble awakening, there is nothing at all to be awakened to.
Just as the four quarters of the realm receive all that has form, [so too does the mind perceive].
Just as [rivers] are all encompassed within the flowing streams, therefore it is called the "sea.
The Ten Powers are likewise so; they are the ocean-seal for all sentient beings.
Having clearly understood their inclinations and natures, they are therefore titled "The Discerning One."
The mind and its intentions are entirely like an illusion; all Buddhas appear as illusory manifestations.
They accord with spontaneous equality, just like that which is produced by an illusion.
The path of the Buddha is entirely a matter of verbal expression, as are all categories of sentient beings.
Fundamentally natural and equal, neither increasing nor diminishing;
there is a most supreme samādhi called the Path of Excellent Awakening.
Abiding amidst the Bodhi tree, one attains this concentrated mind.
Then they manifest radiant brilliance, illuminating infinite multitudes;
opening the Way like a lotus flower, they instruct and transform all sentient beings.
If, in future kalpas, the lands of sentient beings are naturally so, [they shall likewise act].
Contemplation of phenomena is likewise so: regarding all faculties and dispositions with equal vision, one is without self or "mine";
because there is no limit or bottom, one awakens to the covering of the Way.
Practicing the path of a bodhisattva, with vast compassion and wisdom serene, he sat upon the lion throne beneath the tree and attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
His power of the Way is peerless; his Dharma-body is holy and majestic.
Pervasively entering everywhere without exception, they do not abandon sentient beings.
"What is it, O Son of the Buddha, that is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into the wheel of Dharma guided by the Tathāgata’s resonance?"
That Bodhisattva skillfully establishes the Tathāgata’s vast intention, thinking:

"All sentient beings are entirely without beginning or end and have no attainment; they should enter into all phenomena, dwelling forever nowhere, severing [delusion] at its single source, and roaming within the ultimate truth."
"All dharmas are free from the limits of all views; when the limit of desire is relinquished, there is no longer any limit, and one thus enters into the play of all dharmas.

Just as the limit of space is devoid of any mental activity or movement, so too does one enter into the play of all dharmas, which cannot be grasped, for their beginning and end are eternally quiescent."
All dharmas are naturally nirvāṇa; all the expressions of letters and sounds are likewise natural. This is precisely entering into and traversing the wheel of Dharma.
The voice of the Tathāgata pervades all things completely, like the resonance of an echo; thus, that which is spontaneous is the entry into the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
The Dharma-gate is spontaneous: when all sounds become a single resonance, one enters the Wheel of Dharma;
when there is no master over beginning or end and written characters are inexhaustible, one enters the Wheel of Dharma.
Within and without, there is nothing accumulated, just like all the words and expressions expounded through every written character.

Even though such expressions exist, they do not abandon the ultimate truth—whether explaining the past or narrating the beginning and end, all written characters throughout incalculable eons can never be exhausted.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
The wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, consists entirely of provisional designations and mere syllables.

To expound it exhaustively is to have no firm belief, for it is entirely non-existent and beyond all thought; it has no resonance and nothing is bestowed therein. That which turns the wheel of Dharma thus universally enters into all things, yet there is nothing entered.
Just as with provisional words, such as saying "it does not exist" or "a lamp is bright," all that is created is merely based on speech and entirely enters into the realm of numerical categories.
All that is spoken of in the mundane world as transcending the world enters into this [state], where there is forever no abiding.

This voice of the Tathāgata universally enters the realms of all sentient beings, the realm of the bodies of all dharmas, and the matters of retribution and response, yet it forever has no place of abiding.
Whatever various kinds of sounds of speech these multitudes of beings may utter, they all proclaim the sound of the Dharma-wheel of all Tathāgatas. Why is this so?
The wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, issues forth all sounds and resonances without advancing or retreating.
These bodhisattvas enter and traverse the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should establish this and enter into the immeasurable expressions expounded by the Tathāgata.
What are the expressions entered into by the Tathāgata?
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, turns the wheel of Dharma, the sounds he utters accord with the conduct and the inclinations of sentient beings. Why is this?

The Buddha possesses a samādhi called "Unobstructed Ultimate Fearlessness Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. When he enters meditative absorption through this concentration, all sentient beings follow his voice as he turns the wheel of Dharma. From every single mouth of the Perfectly Enlightened One, sounds emerge; from every single word, the awakening of all living beings is manifested, and the echoes of these parables each accord with their respective aspirations.
If one gladdens the hearts of the multitude through this samādhi-samāpatti, this constitutes entering the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata, the Arhat.

Through these gentle and compliant teachings of the Dharma, there is likewise nothing into which one enters; such a course of practice is precisely what constitutes entering this hearing of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, the sacred teachings, and the spoken words. This, O Son of the Buddha, is it!
"The assembly of bodhisattvas enters and traverses the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata to the point of the limitless.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"That wheel is limitless, Accomplishing the ultimate realm."
There is nothing further to be gained, for all things are protected by non-duality;
the various words and letters spoken can never be exhausted,
and the Ten Powers are likewise so— the Wheel of Dharma is eternally inexhaustible.
Expounding upon the teachings of the Vinaya, they enter into all conditioned phenomena,
yet there is nothing into which they enter;
the Buddha-wheel is likewise so.
Entering fully into all modes of speech, yet naturally having nothing to enter,
they universally proclaim to sentient beings all practices without exception.
Transcending conditioned samādhis, they reach the ultimate realization of all meditative states.
Because they seek the sublime Dharma, this is the Buddha’s concentrated mind.
Through the grace bestowed by the Buddha, it reaches all sentient beings;
the voice proclaimed by the Most Victorious One flows forth in gentle and supple words.
With the teaching of a single voice, he proclaims it to all sentient beings;
it is divided into manifold echoes, expounded and chanted without exception.
The Buddha is the Honored One of all; he understands the minds of sentient beings.
Whatever is spoken, the common people hear its sound;
yet characters do not abide within, nor do they arise from without.
When one calculates that all these are utterly extinguished, there is truly nothing at all.
If one turns the wheel of Dharma, it is entirely for the sake of sentient beings;
observe now the ten powers and the transformations they inspire.
From the *Tathāgata-utpatti-saṃdarśana Sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
The Buddha-spoken *Sūtra on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Western Jin period Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.
"What do you mean, Son of the Buddha? How do the Bodhisattvas enter into the manifestation of the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats?"
Regarding "nirvāṇa": when a bodhisattva wishes to enter nirvāṇa and realizes that all things are fundamentally pure and spontaneous, they then become a Buddha.
Just as there is no fundamental basis yet one returns to nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is likewise so.
Furthermore, as with the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), so too is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); it is like the infinite realm of empty space.

Moreover, as with primordial purity, it is like the true primordial limit, yet it is the limit of detachment from desire, the limit of signlessness (*animitta*), and the limit of non-self-nature (*asvabhāva*), just as all dharmas are primordially pure.
Just as the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) attains parinirvāṇa, so too does the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Whether appropriate or inappropriate, all these things are equal and without distinction; they are unarisen and do not originate.
Suppose all dharmas are unarisen and non-emergent; regarding those dharmas, one calculates that there is no going and no not-going, no departing and no not-departing.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not rouse the assembly of bodhisattvas to offer praises and expositions, nor does he cause them to attain parinirvāṇa in ultimate, traceless quiescence.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas stand before one’s very eyes.
Just as it is in the present, so it was in the past and will be in the future; at that very moment, they shall all swiftly attain wisdom and realize the Way in an instant.

Beholding all Tathāgatas, one should proclaim their physical forms and voices; one should give rise neither to dualistic thoughts nor to non-dualistic thoughts. One should abandon all conceptualizations, respond to the conduct of a bodhisattva, and relinquish all attachments.
The Tathāgata does not dwell upon pleasing the minds of the multitude; this is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Out of compassion for the suffering caused by the manifold conceptualizations of sentient beings, he has appeared in the world, yet he does not pass into extinction.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata’s dwelling resides within the Dharma-realm to bring joy to sentient beings; thus he manifests his body and undergoes parinirvāṇa.
The source from which these functions arise is that the Dharma-realm is boundless.
Just as the sun palace emerges from the waters and then universally illumines the entire world,
yet the sun palace has no conceptual thoughts and does not move, while it illuminates everything completely, reaching everywhere without exception.

In all the various vessels filled with water, its reflection is clearly seen; yet when the vessels are lifted and contain no water, or when the light of the sun’s palace is absent, the reflection is no longer seen.
What do you think? Can it be said that this is the fault of the sun, causing its reflection not to appear in the vessels?
He replied: "No.
There is no water; the fault lies with the vessel, not with the sun."
He replied: “It is so.

The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom travels to all realms of phenomena where he has previously gone; for the sake of sentient beings, he constantly expounds purity, brings about spontaneous deeds, leads them to the thought of the Way, and illuminates their minds, such that they always behold the body of the Tathāgata.
Yet those whose vessels are broken and whose minds harbor defilement do not see his majestic radiance.”
O Son of the Buddha!

You should transform and deliver all classes of beings who long for the Tathāgata because they do not see him; therefore, you manifest parinirvāṇa. Yet, there is neither birth nor non-birth, and likewise no parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when the sun shines everywhere, Upon its realm and its distant horizons, The shadow seen is difficult to fear; Once seen, it is no longer seen."
The Honored One among Men appears thus throughout the world;
to sentient beings who lack deep faith, he teaches the Unconditioned.
He universally contemplates all Buddha-lands as being entirely like illusions.
Familiarizing oneself with various causes and conditions, one calculates "self" and "mine.
Even if one were to perform deeds that ultimately constitute the work of a Buddha,
if one does not see the Great Sage, what is perceived will differ.
The Most Victorious One possesses a meditative concentration called "Understanding Impermanence";
having performed his karmic deeds through this, he subsequently manifests equal birth.
By discerning the forms of his body, he makes them immeasurable and limitless.
In an instant, they pervade the ten directions; the Buddha is like a lotus flower.
"He is like fire: for the sake of the world at large, he brings to maturity all that ought to be ripened; yet at another time, in a certain village or district, the fire might suddenly go out."
"What do you think?
Will not all the fires in all worlds be completely extinguished? He replied:
"No," he replied, "in this way, the Tathāgata enters all dharma-realms, pervading them all without exception."

Arising from these Buddha-works, they may at another time manifest the aspiration for the Way in other Buddha-lands; thus they appear to enter parinirvāṇa while not actually entering it—one should, in this manner, enter the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is as if there were a master illusionist who has well studied the arts of illusion, is thoroughly proficient in skillful means, and is fully versed in divine mantras; such a person abides in diligence."

He transforms the entire trichiliocosm so that it all becomes water, yet he manifests his own body within the commanderies, kingdoms, towns, and villages; through his illusory arts, he remains poised over all things and establishes his majestic power, and whenever he wishes to travel to other commanderies, kingdoms, counties, districts, or cities, he simply vanishes by transformation.
"What do you think?
Has the illusion not been completely extinguished? He replied:
"No," he replied. "In this way,

the Tathāgata’s well-awakened illusion of immeasurable wisdom and his spells of skillful means and sacred arts manifest throughout all things, appearing within all dharma-realms, yet there is nothing into which they enter."

It is like a magical illusion: manifesting the body of a Tathāgata that pervades the Dharma-realm and exhausts the limits of space, one then accords with the inclinations and faith of sentient beings, manifesting the lands of various Buddhas and displaying parinirvāṇa, rather than displaying parinirvāṇa in only a single land.
The Tathāgata has fully realized and penetrated all realms of reality;
therefore, O Son of the Buddha, one who is a bodhisattva should know how to enter into the manifestation of the great parinirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses another samādhi called the 'Concentration of Non-attachment and Right Reception Manifesting Great Parinirvāṇa. When he enters right reception through this concentration, from every single pore of the Tathāgata’s body there issue forth incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of radiant beams of light. Each beam of light transforms into lotus flowers beyond counting, and each lotus flower manifests countless, exquisite, and spontaneous lion thrones. Upon these thrones, transformed Tathāgatas sit, each upon their own seat."

The Tathāgata manifests himself in accordance with the categories and numbers of sentient beings; his physical form is complete, and the virtues of ultimate truth are solemn, pure, and fully perfected—all of which are the vows he aspired to in the past.

If there are common people whose faculties are fully matured, they will immediately perceive the Tathāgata’s composed ease and, following the disciplinary teachings, establish a state of solemn purity.
For those among the multitudes whose aspirations for the fundamental limit of the future are matured, they shall be delivered by means of the discipline.
That image of the Tathāgata neither has a location nor lacks a location; it neither speaks nor does not speak; it neither is permanent nor is not permanent.

Furthermore, all of these are the vows and practices undertaken by the Tathāgatas in their past lives; they reveal the path to all sentient beings and fully manifest their various faculties, being entirely the sublime and wondrous transformations produced by their majestic spiritual power.
O Son of the Buddha!

This is how the assembly of bodhisattvas enters the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; their entry is limitless and unimpeded, reaching the ultimate realm of phenomena and the boundless intermediate realm of empty space.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, abiding at the true primordial limit.

When he wishes to manifest, he causes all sentient beings to find rest; through his majestic spiritual power, he establishes them everywhere, revealing the Dharma-realm to all living beings. He transforms their natures in accordance with their capacities and expounds the essentials of the Dharma; though there may be pratyekabuddhas, only bodhisattvas fully comprehend this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

“The Buddha, King of Samādhi, is free from attachment; The Honored One of all sentient beings possesses the power of great compassion, which is boundless, Pervading throughout the aggregates of the body.”
Abiding in the path of true reality, he distinguishes and spreads the rain of Dharma;
its radiant moisture is free from conceptual thought, yet it appears differently to each person throughout the world.
Those who desire to aspire to such wisdom and the minds of those possessed of the ten powers—
Observing the most supreme Sage, by what is the Path defined?
Throughout all the ten directions, regarding all sentient beings and all that has form,
he contemplates them all as empty— without self-nature and without body.
The Bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom transforms into lions and lotuses,
establishing peace and security in various places throughout the dharma-realm of sentient beings.
All dwell securely in the noble state, spontaneously accomplishing wise strategy.
By means of this boundless wisdom, one transcends all embodied existence.
Being already equally liberated, within the dharma-realm there are no persons or things;
throughout the ten directions, this is where the pratyekabuddhas dwell.
Only thus, O Son of the Buddha!
Is there penetration of the dharma-realm without remainder; furthermore, one observes all dharma-realms as neither increasing nor diminishing.
One who draws near to the most supreme Sage, Who possesses mastery over all wisdom—
Whether training or not training, In the conditioned and the unconditioned;
All those who dwell in mastery, Neither diminishing nor increasing anything.
Exhaustless and without arising, the Buddha’s wisdom is beyond limit.
Like the flow of water, it gradually and sequentially pervades all,
moistening and softening the earth.
That water is without flattery or deceit, and the earth likewise has no conceptual thought, yet it causes the water not to be all-pervasive.
By practicing the power of diligence, one extensively discerns everything;
with the ten powers that are boundless, one understands the realms of all sentient beings.
These multitudes of living beings, contemplating and dwelling securely in wisdom,
shall accordingly follow and practice it, establishing the work of diligence;
knowing that this will not be long, they shall build up the wisdom of merit.
"What do you mean, Son of the Buddha?
When a bodhisattva hears what the Tathāgata has manifested, how should they enter into the foundation of all virtues?
By means of these inexhaustible true practices, the bodhisattva does not view the Tathāgata through falsehood."
Furthermore, having heard what was taught, they plant the roots of all virtues and enter into immeasurable practices of desire, mastering them through ultimate spiritual power with equanimity.
Born within the conditioned world, they universally fulfill all vows without exhaustion;
they roam and enter the unconditioned, yet when they manifest activity for the sake of the future, it is without limit.
Having reached the ultimate limit of form and desire, one attains the stage of sovereign mastery.
It is like a person who attempts to destroy a diamond with a mere puff of wind; although such a person acts thus, they cannot bring about its destruction or increase its flaws.
One should contemplate that its substance is an impure vessel, wherein the five viscera are dispersed and entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, as for that wind, it is a natural law that there is destruction and decay.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!
Following the teachings of the Tathāgata from the Buddha-dharma, even those who have planted meager roots of virtue all destroy the afflictions in which they dwell within all conditioned phenomena.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is unconditioned and entirely non-existent; it eliminates all obstructions, and the roots of all the virtues cultivated by the Tathāgata are never extinguished.

It is just as if someone were to pile up firewood and grass as high as Mount Sumeru, and a mustard-seed-sized spark of fire were thrown upon that wood; it would be instantly consumed entirely, leaving nothing behind.
Why is this so? It is because the nature of fire is to burn whatever it encounters.

In the same way, a practitioner, though they may plant but a small amount of merit within the lineage of the Tathāgata, completely burns away all afflictions (*kleśa*) until nothing remains, swiftly attaining proximity to and taking refuge in *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? It is because they have forever and completely exhausted all obscurations and hindrances;
having planted the roots of virtue within the lineage of the Tathāgata, they have extinguished all defilements.

It is like a great medicine named Sudarśana; if one beholds its color, hears its sound, smells its fragrance, consumes it, or wears its form, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind naturally attain purity.
Furthermore, if at the end it enters the earth and transforms into medicinal herbs, it then heals diseases once again.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is like a great king of physicians; endowed with noble wisdom, he benefits sentient beings and provides healing for many.
If one beholds the form-body (rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata, the eyes become pure;
if the ears hear the samādhi, one attains far-reaching hearing;
if one smells the fragrance of the precepts, the nose naturally becomes pure.
By partaking of the flavor of the Dharma, they are satiated with all practices;
those who hear what the Tathāgata preaches find their tongues naturally purified and possess immeasurable eloquence;
and those who encounter the radiance of the Tathāgata immediately attain the Dharma-body.
Those who bring the Tathāgata to mind will have minds that are equally pure;
those who make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, will establish the roots of virtue and eliminate the afflictions of toil and dust.
"Now, O Son of the Buddha! I exhort and reveal this:
those who see or hear the Tathāgata are able to purify and eliminate the afflictions of the aggregates and their karmic transgressions."

If there are those who, upon seeing, hearing, or being taught, lack joy and faith, the Buddha causes them to plant and perfect the roots of virtue so that it shall not be in vain, until they attain *nirvāṇa*.

Those who see the Tathāgata or hear his voice enter into the foundation of all virtues; by this, they sever all unwholesome dharmas and universally realize the source of all paths, lacking nothing, and are entirely liberated.
He draws upon various parables; yet the Tathāgata’s manifestation is such that all things are fully present within him, making it impossible to employ parables as mere provisional metaphors.
The Buddha’s merit is inconceivable; he gives rise to the mind of deliverance, desiring to transform the dispositions and natures of all sentient beings so that they may attain joy.
For this reason, the Tathāgata employs various parables for the sake of the bodhisattvas, desiring to lead them to understanding; however, these are not the essential core.

Such a grand principle is the secret and profound treasury of the Tathāgata; it is called that which is beyond the comprehension of all the world, and it constitutes entry into the wondrous seal of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata possesses great wisdom and the lineage of boundless, holy illumination; he is named the one whom all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings cannot equal; he is named the one who enters and dwells in the realm of equality that is the domain of the Tathāgata; he is named the one who purifies the realms of all beings until none remain; and he is named the one who universally expounds the origins of all things and all points of obstruction.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not preach this sublime scripture for others; he expounds the Bodhisattva path only for those who aspire to the Great Vehicle and seek the inconceivable vehicle.
Furthermore, this sutra never returns to other destinies for any bodhisattvas. "O Son of the Buddha!

It is just as when the seven natural treasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King—the golden wheel, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, the bright pearl, the jade woman, the minister of the treasury, and the minister of the army—appear through such a transformation; they do not go to anyone else, but proceed only to the crown prince of the king."
Why is this? Because he was born from the womb of a noble queen, he is fully endowed as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
If a principal queen gives birth to such a crown prince, he is fully endowed with the marks of a sage king.
When his life comes to an end, the seven treasures belonging to the Wheel-Turning Sage King will all vanish after seven days and no longer appear; thus there will be nothing remaining.

In this same manner, the root of the sūtras shall ultimately never go to others, but shall reach only the eldest son of Perfect Enlightenment, those born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, and those who have planted the roots of merit of the Tathāgata.
Even if one reaches the Dharma-body, a practitioner who follows the path shall receive its grace; though their momentum cannot last long, they shall surely attain accomplishment.
Such is this physical form—the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and the essence of the scriptures—which ensures that the Three Jewels are not severed.
If the Dharma were to perish entirely, there would be no one left to behold it.
Why is this? Because all those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles are incapable of bearing it; they have not even heard the sound of this sutra, let alone receive, uphold, recite, or read it.
One should take refuge solely in the great beings, the bodhisattvas; their writings shall be kept in scrolls and reverently placed within one's dwelling.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

If there is a bodhisattva who hears this exposition, and whose disposition is humble and sincere as they respectfully attend the Dharma Master and provide for his needs and comfort, that person should receive this scripture.
Why is this so? Suppose there is a bodhisattva who possesses profound faith and takes [the Buddha] as his model, destined to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

Even if such a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to practice and accumulate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) for incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of eons, and further bring forth the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and cultivate compassion—yet if he does not enter into this infinite and inconceivable state of the Tathāgata, neither hearing it nor progressing toward it, he cannot be called a bodhisattva. He provides no benefit or growth to the bodhisattva-dharmas, and thus does not follow the lineage of the Tathāgata.

If there is a bodhisattva who expounds the unimpeded wisdom of all Tathāgatas, entering the Way with firm faith and without hesitation, this one is called a true bodhisattva. Such a person does not deviate from or lose the power of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and is universally able to bring to ultimate completion the great sage-like practices of all worldly dharmas. Following the teachings of the Tathāgata, they remain unattached within the realms of all Buddhas, successfully establishing all bodhisattva dharmas, and attaining penetration into the correct scriptures of all Buddhas without any lingering doubt.

The realms of the factors of enlightenment undergo many transformations; through the attainment of mastery, one establishes all dharmas, and amidst the towering spiritual power of the bodhisattvas, one immediately enters the unimpeded realm of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, if a bodhisattva hears this Dharma, they will universally attain and abide in the infinite resolve for the Way.

Furthermore, when their power and momentum of aspiration reach the ultimate truth, they cast off all manifold conceptions—whether appropriate or inappropriate—and enter into holy wisdom, wherein all Tathāgatas appear as if before their very eyes.
That which is to be contemplated is the thorough understanding of the realm of empty space, the honoring of samādhi, and the opening and awakening of the mind.

Those who enter the immeasurable dharma-realm act according to the resolve of all bodhisattvas; they accomplish myriad virtues and attain mastery, reaching full proficiency in supernormal wisdom, removing the manifold defilements of the world, and generating the aspiration for enlightenment without remainder.

That land pervades all the ten directions; entering the path of the bodhisattva, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are unified as a single way. Equally pursuing the roots of virtue, they assist the holy path, guiding and benefiting all sentient beings so that they may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, and transforming those who have not yet heard it so that they shall enter this Dharma.
Entering that which has no entry, they find no opportunity for affliction; they cause all dharmas to return to the absence of causes and conditions, constantly forming this thought:
"I shall accord with all-knowledge and all dharmas."
"All these are infinite.

When a bodhisattva has already been able to enter and roam within such states, that which they contemplate becomes a minor matter; their entry is difficult to reach, their wisdom is sovereign, and their majestic spiritual power is sublime.

When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, having received the holy command of the Buddha, spoke this Dharma, immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions—equal in number to the atoms of dust—trembled in six ways, and eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations manifested as a response.

As the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power fully manifested the gift of Dharma, celestial flowers rained down; lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; garments, ornaments, parasols, canopies, and banners were scattered; and the rain of various fragrances surpassed all the famous perfumes, blended incenses, ground incenses, and celestial necklaces found in the heavens.
Furthermore, great wish-fulfilling jewels rained down, and their radiance surpassed all that is treasured by the devas.
It was praised, saying:
"Excellent! The path of the Bodhisattva surpasses that of all devas; it is eternally formless and cannot be grasped."
Furthermore, the various bodhisattvas, drawing upon their own past merits, rained down a pervasive shower of rare and wondrous jewels—an inconceivable, pure adornment.

Having attained supreme perfect enlightenment in the buddha-fields, they all gathered like clouds, raining down immeasurable Dharma, chanting with elegant and melodic voices, and extolling the words and teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas—just as when a bodhisattva first attains perfect enlightenment in the four great realms, establishing, initiating, and bringing to fruition the path of bodhisattvas so as to cause them joy.

In this way, throughout all Buddha-worlds without exception, extending in every direction across the ten quarters, there are incalculable eighty *koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasra* Buddha-lands; the dust motes filling them each exceed the number of such Buddha-lands.
The Buddhas of the present behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and hearing what he preaches, they praise him from afar, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of noble family!"
This is what the Tathāgata has analyzed and taught as inconceivable.
Why is this so? Because he establishes the ultimate truth and enters into the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—eighty incalculable billions of trillions of Buddha-fields filled with atoms as many as there are—all Buddhas spontaneously produce sounds to preach the Dharma, saying:
"We here now proclaim and instruct you; just as our own followers have been enlightened and transformed, so too is the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas equal and without distinction."

Furthermore, if all bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of lands, were to attain supernatural powers and enter various samādhis, and because they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions who are about to bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment, they would all obtain the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha) and return to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

Sentient beings as numerous as the dust motes filling the lands of a thousand buddhas have resolved their minds toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path; they have all been granted predictions of enlightenment by the Holy Honored One. In the future, throughout kalpas as numerous as the dust motes filling countless buddha-lands, they shall all attain buddhahood, receiving the titles Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and "The One Who Is Like the Buddha-Land. They shall constantly establish this Dharma, preaching that which bodhisattvas of the future have never heard before, proclaiming and putting it into practice so that all sentient beings in the four quarters of every world may know it.
Just as the multitudes of beings in this realm are covered by grace, enlightened by the Way and its teachings, and made to conform to the precepts;

so too it is in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. Hundreds of billions, trillions—immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, boundless—all those sentient beings within the realms of the Buddhas throughout the entirety of empty space are universally enlightened. This is brought about by the majestic spiritual power and illuminating light of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and by what was established through the Tathāgatas' past roots of virtue; they have attained all dharmas and cultivate the foundations of merit.

The noble wisdom of the Tathāgata is beyond all comparison; the Buddha’s teaching guides and benefits beings according to the time, universally governing them so that the various bodhisattvas obtain what is appropriate for their needs, their faculties become disciplined and settled, and the practices performed in past lives are never lost.

The majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is vast and expansive; he is the embodiment of all-pervasive wisdom, majesty, and benevolence. All the bodhisattvas throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of buddha-lands in the ten directions—whose number is as vast as the dust motes filling those lands—have thus gathered together in this assembly, pervading the realms of all dharmas across the ten directions.
He manifests the infinite adornment and purity of a bodhisattva, radiating great light that moves all buddha-worlds;
he startles the celestial palaces and subdues the hosts of Māras, extinguishing all evils and the various realms of existence.

He proclaimed the immeasurable majesty and honor of the Tathāgata, praising the virtues of the Tathāgata with the incalculable joy of all dharmas; from his lute he produced infinite sounds that rained down upon all, without limit or bottom, manifesting the most extraordinary jewels and various kinds of offerings in infinite variety.

Each with a distinct body, they all became vessels for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate; receiving immeasurable teachings as the capacity of their own bodies allowed, they followed the holy intent of the Buddha and, with one voice in unison, proclaimed these words of equal resonance:
“Excellent, excellent! You are the sons of the Buddha, and you are thus able to proclaim the peerless Dharma of the Tathāgata.”

Furthermore, all that they have practiced accords with Samantabhadra; they have attained immeasurable renown and entered into the resonance of sounds and names, having come here personally from the presence of the Tathāgata.
That Buddha-world is named Universal Radiance (Samantaraśmi), and its Dharma is likewise so.
Now, there is no difference between them; they all preach this Dharma, having received the holy intent of the Buddha and attained the scriptures of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
Bear witness that those established by the Buddhas of the present have come to this assembly.
"Furthermore, just as those who have now arrived at this assembly, so too are the infinite beings taught throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions; all are identical to space.

In the buddha-lands of all the various realms and regions of the four quarters, the buddha-lands established by the Tathāgata are displayed as being immeasurable. The bodhisattvas who come from hundreds of thousands of buddha-lands, filling them like motes of dust, are all due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, having cultivated peerless virtues."
"By means of these verses, he is thus adorned; being thoroughly examined, he is without flaw and none can surpass him.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva fully observed the virtues of all bodhisattvas;
having scrutinized the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*), he proclaimed the lineage of the Great Sage.

The principle elucidates the boundless Way of all Buddhas; the Dharma of the Tathāgata is without peer. Thus, he extols its vast and infinite reach, for it is entirely rooted in past virtues and fundamental merits that analyze and illuminate all formless realms.

He expounds the Buddhist scriptures, universally understanding the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, perceiving them all without exception, and causing the masses to attain them; he enables them to grasp the phrases of the Dharma at the appropriate time without abandoning them.
He causes the bodhisattvas to contemplate the immeasurable radiance of the path of the Dharma, comprehending it with thorough and refined mastery.
The World-Honored One establishes boundlessness without pride, manifesting speech and song; all Tathāgatas are but a single body, unified within one Dharma-body.
Furthermore, he proclaimed the great practices of his past lives; the power of his diligence was unrestrained, and the force of his auspiciousness was equal to the limits of existence.
Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, that which is moved by the Way is beyond analogy; it is reached only through the ineffable.
At that time, Samantabhadra addressed him again, saying:

"There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*). By being fully endowed with this patience of dharmas, one is free from the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandhāvaraṇa*), thereby reaching the stage of all-dharma-patience, wherein there is no obstruction regarding the teachings of all Buddhas."

What are these ten? First, penetration of sounds; second, compliant practice; third, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; fourth, likened to an illusion; fifth, likened to a mirage; sixth, likened to a dream; seventh, likened to an echo; eighth, likened to a shadow; ninth, likened to a transformation; tenth, likened to space. These are the ten dharmic patiences attained by a bodhisattva.
"What, then, is meant by 'patience toward sounds' (ghoṣānugakṣānti)?

To hear whatever sounds one may encounter without harboring fear, without dread, and without anxiety; to joyfully contemplate and comply with them; and to practice all that is followed accordingly without any transgression—this is patience toward sounds."
"What is meant by 'patience in accord with the Dharma' (anulomika-dharma-kṣānti)?
It is when a bodhisattva, in accordance with the arising of dharmas that should be traversed, observes those dharmas and establishes practices and so forth, without creating opposition or confusion."
If all dharmas are such that they should be compliant, one should deliver those who are to be delivered.

With a pure disposition and nature, practicing equanimity and applying diligent effort, entering into and accomplishing compliance—this is the patience of the dharma of compliance (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena?
It is that when a bodhisattva perceives any phenomena that arise, they find them to have no locus whatsoever; they do not calculate their cessation, nor do they perceive anything at all."

That which is unarisen has nothing that can be extinguished; that which is without extinction has nothing that can be exhausted; that which is without exhaustion has nothing that can be destroyed; that which is without destruction has no limit or bottom; that which has no bottom is the ground of stillness; that which is the ground of stillness is serenity; that which is serene has no activity; that which has no activity has no aspiration—this is called the non-arising third dharma-patience.
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the illusion-like nature of all phenomena?
It is to understand clearly that all phenomena are like illusions, produced through causes and conditions.

To have firm faith in the single dharma that delivers countless and immeasurable dharmas; to enter into the single dharma by means of innumerable dharmas; to enter into the self and to enter into the non-entering; and to be entirely without attachment to all established teachings and the guidance of various practices."
It is like a great elephant atop a multitude of vehicles; as an illusion, it does not dwell together with elephants, chariots, cavalry, or infantry;
it does not dwell together with men, women, boys, or girls, whether large or small;
nor does it dwell together with trees, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits.
When a bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are like illusions, they neither conjoin nor disperse; they do not dwell together with earth, water, fire, or wind;
they do not dwell together with day and night, the fifteen-day fortnight, the month, or the year;
they do not calculate hundreds or thousands of years, nor do they dwell together with the cycles of days, months, or kalpas.
He does not dwell or associate with those who see things through the lens of shadows and echoes;
he does not dwell or associate with those who perceive things as manifold or as non-manifold; he does not dwell or associate with those who enter into a single matter by means of manifoldness;
he does not dwell or associate with those who are either sublime or base, or who are gentle or harsh.
He does not dwell or associate with those who are few or many;
he does not dwell or associate with those who are finite or infinite;
nor does he dwell or associate with various diverse assemblies that share the same physical form.
Those in the assembly do not dwell together with illusory transformations, nor do those illusory transformations dwell together with the assembly.
There is no dwelling and no non-dwelling, and there is nowhere they do not dwell; yet they equally deliver all views and the various distinct illusory perceptions.
In this state, there is ultimately nothing to be seen through any views; rather, one perceives the fundamental source of all realms of existence. O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into the world by means of the illusory-like.

The world of worldly afflictions, the world of mundane customs and practices in lands, the world of the self, the world of sensation and perception, the world of the conditioned, the world of detachment from existence, the world of conjunction, the world of non-conjunction, the world of conceptual discrimination, and the world of volitional formations—these are the names for the worlds that Bodhisattvas deliver.

Thus, one manifests as an illusory transformation, universally entering all worlds; yet one does not grasp at sentient beings, nor does one destroy sentient beings; one does not grasp at lands, nor does one ruin lands; one does not grasp at dharmas, nor does one destroy dharmas. One does not dwell on past events, nor does one form conceptions regarding the past, nor is one devoid of conception. There is no future, nor is there the performance of conditioned actions. One does not fall into the unarisen, does not abide in the present, and does not destroy what exists. Thus, one does not race toward the Buddha-way, nor does one conceptualize the Way. One neither associates with Buddhas nor exhorts Buddhas to enter parinirvāṇa. One does not abide in various vows, yet does not abandon one's pledges. One cultivates equality, yet does not engage in the adornment or purification [of realms], remaining free from all obstructions.
He opens the way to the buddha-lands and exhorts others to enter them; he remains unbroken and unmoving within the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

He enters equally into the notions of self and does not contradict or destroy the perception of a self; he instructs all practices regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), eliminates all attachments, and brings sentient beings across to liberation.
Regarding these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one has no dependence or attachment; one clearly understands that all dharmas are entirely equal and ultimately unattainable.
The differentiation of dharmas is merely a matter of provisional designations; regarding the clear wisdom of noble penetration, there is nothing that can pass away.
To deliver sentient beings while always acting in accordance with the appropriate timing, yet without relying on the causal conditions of those beings;

to abide in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and fully expound the matters of past deeds and their inconceivable retributions, causing all to believe and understand—this is the fourth Dharma-patience, the Parable of Illusion.
"What is meant, O Son of the Buddha,
by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s patience regarding the nature of a mirage?
It is that the Bodhisattva understands that all things in the world are entirely illusory, just like a mirage seen by people from afar."
Just as rivers flow and waves arise, yet the wise understand that there is no water in the shimmering heat;

so it is with the Bodhisattva, who discerns the various phenomena of existence and non-existence, neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, neither subject to annihilation nor reckoned as eternal, and does not enter into the state of disparaging or being disparaged by the teachings.
Observing that things exist as if they were present yet there are no evil realms, the mind does not turn outward nor abide within.
Whether appearing as a single form or manifold forms, one knows them to be without form.
That all dharmas are fully endowed with subtlety and are entirely without origin— this is the fifth dharma-patience,
"Like a Mirage. "What, O Son of the Buddha,
is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s patience regarding the analogy of dreams?"
The Bodhisattva contemplates the world as being like a dream; just as a person in a dream does not abide in the world, does not arise from the world, and is not born from the world.
Furthermore, in a dream, there is no desire realm, nor is there a form realm, nor is there a formless realm.
Therefore it is said that in a dream there is nothing produced and nothing at all exists; since a dream has no afflictions, there is no fetter or resentment.
Furthermore, when one examines a dream, it neither arises nor is it pure; in a dream, one does not see a dream.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates all worlds as being clearly understood to be like a dream; there is neither illumination nor darkness therein. The dreamer is spontaneous, and the dream is without attachment; the dreamer is ethereal and the dreamer is fundamentally pure. It is because something is established that this dream exists.
A dream has nothing that can be destroyed; it exists because of the thoughts and conceptions one harbors.
If one can understand that all phenomena are like dreams and thereby guide the world, this is the sixth dharma-patience, "Like a Dream."
"What is meant, O Son of the Buddha, by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s patience regarding the dharma of echoes?

When a Bodhisattva studies the Dharma, whatever sounds they enter and whatever they learn, they deliver those who have not yet been delivered; through their study of the Dharma, they transform and enlighten others, fully comprehending all things."
It is like an echo: it is not that there is no sound, yet fundamentally all is quiescent, and there is nothing to be measured.

In this way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes the internal and external echoes of the Tathāgata; he does not perceive internal or external phenomena as distinct, nor does he know the external, nor does he use the internal to comprehend external things. Seeing no basis for reliance, he understands the propriety of speech, advancement, and retreat; this is what is meant by understanding various chapters and phrases.
Causes and conditions are like echoes that provide guidance; in the gift of all dharmas, there is nothing they do not penetrate, nor is there any obstruction.
As for those who learn, they discern and understand that all sounds are ultimately non-existent.
It is like the exquisite celestial maidens who attend upon Śakra, Lord of Devas, who simultaneously produce the sounds of hundreds of thousands of musical instruments from a single mouth and body.
Furthermore, those musicians have no conceptual thoughts, nor does their speech harbor the thought:
"I am now producing hundreds of thousands of wondrous sounds.

Likewise, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas transcend all realms, they are without conceptualization and without verbal expression; yet, through their mastery of skillful means (*upāya*), they produce immeasurable sounds, employing limitless expedients within the worldly dharmas without ever retreating.

Constantly turning the wheels of the various realms among the multitudes of beings, he expounds them in detail for those gathered; providing much guidance and instruction, he establishes them. His speech flows forth as unimpeded sounds, manifesting throughout all Buddha-lands to inspire faith and joy.

He proclaims the scriptures and instructs the masses, exerting his radiant light to illuminate those who have not yet awakened, causing them all to realize the nature of all sounds; though he may speak, nothing that he says is ever produced.

Wandering through various sounds without any conceptualization, they further provide guidance, understanding that nothing is produced, proclaiming the sites of awakening, and reaching the path of the sages.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these states of non-attainment, causing all who hear them to enter into what is raised by all Buddhas, to behold the Buddhas face-to-face as they turn the infinite wheel of Dharma for those to be saved, and to accord with non-conceptualization—this is the seventh Dharma-patience, known as "Like an Echo."
"What is meant, O Son of the Buddha,
by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s 'patience like a reflection' (*pratibhāsa-dharma-kṣānti*)?

It is when the bodhisattva does not sink into the world, is not born into the world, does not wander in the world, does not emerge from the world, does not act within the world, does not believe in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and yet does not destroy conventional practice."
Furthermore, regarding the world, there is neither its non-destruction, nor its arrival in the world, nor craving for the world, nor governing the world, nor prolonging existence in the world.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not abide in the world, nor does he transcend the world; nor does he practice the conduct of a bodhisattva. He has no fixed conviction, and regarding his great vows, they are neither unreal nor real, neither existent nor non-existent.

Being free from false and delusive conduct, one proceeds toward the Dharma of all Buddhas, pervading the entire world without exception; yet one dwells in nothing within worldly dharmas and does not follow worldly teachings.

It is like a shadow; it is as if it were the sun’s palace, or as the moon’s illumination upon men, women, trees, mountains, houses, the various palaces of the gods, and the many forms of rivers and streams—its immeasurable causes and conditions are inexhaustible.
In all directions, by means of the light of the sun, one beholds all forms and knows their destinations as clearly as in pure water.
Furthermore, it is like a boatman or a luminous jewel, which, by virtue of what is seen, allows for complete mastery.

In this regard, those who are worthy of what is offered according to their inclinations—even those who are impure and lack radiance—all receive its light; yet even as they receive this illumination, there is nothing created therein.
Furthermore, that radiance is also non-existent—it has no sound and is not produced—yet it is by means of that radiance that distinctions are made.
Yet that radiance has no place of abiding; though it is pure and manifest, it does not coexist with purity and manifestation.

Even when situated upon a ground of radiance, it is called "radiance," yet while illuminating various flows, there is nothing illuminated, and thus there is no pervasion. Its reflection likewise does not enter rivers, springs, great oceans, or deep pools.
Furthermore, one calculates that its shadow has no location and nothing to which it adheres; the manifestation of that shadow is neither bright and pure nor possessed of blemish.
When this shadow does not appear, then within that interval one does not rely upon or grasp a fundamental basis;
when the shadow appears extensively, there is neither distance nor proximity.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva has reached the nature of those whom he transforms; his aspirations and conduct proceed with mastery.

Regarding the field of the wisdom of the path for all sentient beings he observes, he encourages others in their own aspirations and practices, treating them all equally without distinction. He discerns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in which he himself dwells, thoroughly examining his own realm and the realms of others as being entirely non-dual."
It is like a planter of trees: from the initial sprouting of the bud, it gradually flourishes and grows, eventually producing stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit.

In this way, when a bodhisattva discerns the various characteristics of both their own dharma-realm and the realms of others, and realizes that dharmas are non-dual, they then transcend and enter the unimpeded primordial limit.

That bodhisattva’s body then transcends inconceivable Buddha-lands; though seeing those Buddha-lands, he has no attachment to them, nor does he shift among those worlds, and even when reaching the realms of the Buddhas, he arrives nowhere.
The reach of the Dharma-body is like the shadow of the sun’s chariot, which is fully present wherever it goes; its body enters everywhere, manifesting in all realms.
Wherever it manifests birth, its activity is unimpeded, yet it neither divides its body nor has any place of going.

There is no such thing as worldly conventional thought; one eliminates the empty and nihilistic rhetoric of various lands, yet does not disperse the body, attaining that which has neither end nor beginning, encompassing all things without exception.

The lineage of the Tathāgata and the conduct of its primordial limit do not further purify the actions of body, speech, and mind; rather, one immediately attains entry into and praise of the immeasurable, purifying all bodies such that there is nowhere they do not pervade. This is the eighth Dharma-patience, known as "Like a Reflection."
“What, O Son of the Buddha, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding the dharma of being like an illusion?

The bodhisattva universally enters into the mundane world; wherever he goes, he contemplates and realizes that all sentient beings are like illusions, yet he does not falsely perceive them, maintaining mindfulness of things as being like illusions.”

What is called "transformation" refers to all worlds of existence, which are produced by conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and transformed by mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*); these are all categories of such transformations as suffering, pleasure, and perversions.

All worlds are entirely conditioned by ignorance; through thought and reflection, they give rise to the various conceptualizations of worldly toil (*kleśa*). Born through these causes and conditions, there are established and proclaimed the sounds, resonances, and the principles of the Dharma.

They transform them through the teaching of non-conceptualization, making them firm and non-retrogressive; they guide them toward equanimity, awaken them from all states of non-awakening, cause them to establish their resolve and vows, and act like those who have undergone spiritual transformation.

Observing the Tathāgata’s practice of great compassion, the multitudes who are born through transformation understand this: namely, the cultivation of the wheel of Dharma through skillful means, and mastery in the noble penetration of wisdom, fearlessness, and the four analytical eloquences.

In this way, the Bodhisattva transforms and delivers the world; his supramundane merit, eloquence, and sovereign mastery are vast and boundless. Entering among assemblies of immeasurable billions, he dwells therein with complete freedom, being able to fully comprehend the conduct of humans and the movements of devas, and perceiving where the path of the sages does not exist, he reveals the Great Way so that their practice is never at variance with it.
For example, a magically conjured person has no thoughts and performs no actions;
they do not give rise to mental activities, nor do they dwell upon any phenomena. They do not arise from karma, nor do they hope for retribution.
They have no place to which they travel, they do not emerge from the world, nor do they attain perfect enlightenment within the world, nor do they even think of the Dharma.
Not practicing any dharmas, neither abiding for long nor for a moment; having no fixed location and not engaging in worldly customs;
not extending through the world and without words of direction; not approaching any limits, yet having no limitlessness;
neither increasing nor decreasing; having no firm conviction, yet no lack thereof.
Faith is neither noble nor ordinary; it is neither affliction nor resentment.
It does not perish, nor is it born. It is neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom; it is neither existent nor subtle.
It does not rely upon the world, nor does it lead or govern. Regarding all things...
The Dharma-realm is neither wise nor ignorant; it neither receives nor does not receive.
It has no five aggregates, yet it is not without aggregates; it has no birth and death, yet it is not nirvana; it is neither existent nor non-existent.

In this way, the bodhisattva wanders through the world, cultivating the bodhisattva practices, possessing clear understanding and eloquence, and not giving rise to arrogance; beholding the world, he is free from self-conceit and adheres to his own practice.

Not for one’s own sake, nor for the sake of the mundane world, being without negligence, they are without a self and free from attachment and pride; neither relying on this nor depending on the mundane, they abandon arrogance and indulgence and are free from conceptualization. They do not abide in the world, yet they do not sever the world; they do not exercise mastery over phenomena to excess, nor do they have any clinging attachment to the realm of persons. They provide no guidance, nor do they abide in the realm of sentient beings; they have no aspirations, no conceptualizations, and no purification.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to adorn; the dharmas of all Buddhas are entirely non-existent, yet they fully accomplish even the Great Way.
Moreover, these dharmas neither exist nor do not exist, just as those transformations neither exist nor do not exist.

“The Bodhisattva who has attained transformation dwells in the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti) and equally understands all Buddha-ways; having achieved this, he establishes the ultimate truth. This is the Bodhisattva’s comprehensive grasp of the Buddha-dharma: like a transformation, it has no location, and throughout the Buddha-way, there is nothing to be acquired.”

The conduct of sentient beings is free from the hindrances of the aggregates; they do not give rise to the notion of a self-body, yet they enter into all bodies to guide them, establishing themselves therein without any attachment.
If one perceives forms, one regards forms as like illusions, remaining entirely without attachment while being fully endowed with equanimity;
the natural radiance of the ultimate reality illuminates all, such that one does not rely upon the dharma of liberation;
regarding all phenomena, they appear to arise while fundamentally being without arising.

Just as that emanated person has no conscious recollection and is pure by nature, so too when receiving words, one should speak in accordance with what is taught, following all laws without any conceptualization.

Like a magical transformation, produced through change and alteration, they manifest their arrival here at the sublime site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of all Tathāgatas; free from conditions for regression and without anything arising, they act without obstruction, perfect all powers, and are entirely devoid of conceptual thought.
Just as that emanated person’s mind penetrates everything without being obstructed or hindered by the mountain that encircles the gods—this is the ninth Dharma-patience, "Like an Emanation.
"What, O Son of the Buddha, is meant by this?"
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attain the patience regarding the dharma that is like space?
The Bodhisattva contemplates entering the realm of sentient beings as being like empty space, devoid of any causal characteristics;
all dharmas and the multitudes of phenomena are likewise thus.
Entering the lands of all Buddhas yet without any fixed reality, for all dharmas are empty and devoid of duality; the Bodhisattva thus enters that which is without vows.
Just as empty space encompasses all Buddha-lands, so it is with this state—free from bondage or attachment—one gives rise to the power entered by the Tathāgatas and wanders together with them.
Just as space is non-dual in that which enters it, so too is the Path—without past, future, or present;
and wisdom is likewise. Thus, all dharmas are explained through discernment as entering into suchness.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), it is like empty space; the noble wisdom they achieve is likewise so.
Whatever they attain through these various vehicles is entirely like empty space, such that they achieve mastery over body, speech, and mind.
Just as space, the various dharmas attained are accomplished through what is conceived by the mind.
Just as space does not plant seeds within any dharma, neither perishing nor arising;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who attains mastery over all dharmas, having neither end nor beginning.
It is like space: it has no location and nothing can destroy it; likewise, within all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, there is no location and nothing can be destroyed.
Within the powers of the Buddhas, it abides spontaneously like space, yet it dwells nowhere in any world; this is the realm of spontaneity.
In this way, the Bodhisattva establishes sentient beings, yet there is nothing established, for all things are like transformations.
Just as space neither arises nor ceases and has no place of birth, yet encompasses all that exists within every world;
so too the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no abiding place, no achievement, and yet there is that which is adorned and purified, because he universally manifests all worlds.
Just as space has no location and no directions, no boundaries and no depths, being vast and profound, reaching everywhere without exception;

so it is with the Bodhisattva, who has no location and no directions yet reaches everywhere, proclaiming and penetrating the expansiveness of all dharmas, equally governing all practices without anything left unpermeated.
Just as space, though it has no place of abiding or support upon which to stand, gives rise to nothing yet manifests the myriad forms of all sentient beings;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: they neither act nor abide, yet they move in accordance with the conduct of the multitudes, manifesting themselves while remaining without any origination.
Just as space has no form and yet no lack of form, no pure conduct and yet no defilement, because it is governed by the Way; so too is the Bodhisattva:
they have no mundane form, no supramundane form, and no immeasurable form, yet they manifest because there is that which causes them to appear.
"Just as space has neither long-term stability nor even a moment's duration,
so too the bodhisattva does not endure for long and does not abide for even a moment."
It is like manifesting a reflection while having no reflection; if a bodhisattva understands this in their practice, they shall attain the ultimate.
Their practice is like space: they manifest all afflictions (*kleśa*) without defilement, and manifest all fetters and resentments without hatred.

When a bodhisattva is thus, they subdue all Māras through the power of the Way; all things are pure, their mind is fresh and clean, tranquil and serene, universally encompassing everything that exists in the world.
Furthermore, just as space encompasses the world without distinction or partiality,
so too does the bodhisattva treat all phenomena with complete equanimity.
Moreover, the bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters no obstruction regarding any phenomena, nor does he suffer any loss.
Just as space pervades all things equally, and one cannot limit space because it has no boundaries;
so too the Bodhisattva, with respect to all phenomena, dwells in the simultaneous movement of both will and nature.
Furthermore, that mind of the Way has no boundaries. Why is this?
Because that which is empty space is equal throughout its extent.

When a bodhisattva adheres to practice within themselves, accomplishing purity and establishing equanimity as a single cycle of activity, they then transform a single matter into the immeasurable and travel universally through all lands.

If one is like empty space, reaching no ultimate limit within all Buddha-lands yet attaining full perfection; dwelling nowhere among all directions, yet entering all quarters to accomplish supernormal powers; naturally endowed with all virtues and immeasurable, extraordinary matters; fully obtaining the *pāramitās* of all dharmas, attaining the art of firmness, and having a will like empty space.
If one is like a vajra, having no conceptualization regarding any sound, and guides all voices accordingly, then one does not deviate from or abandon the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

If a bodhisattva’s practice can fully accomplish this kind of patience, then they attain mastery; yet there is nowhere to which they go, no departing and no arriving, and being entirely without any destination, they attain mastery without anything to be extinguished.

Thus, one attains mastery over the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through one's own effort; with nothing lost—save for the unreal body—one accomplishes the true essence in accordance with the teachings of the Vinaya.
When the mind has no expectations, it becomes a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*); when that body is autonomous and enters the signless (*animitta*), then by means of the signless, it is without limit.

The Buddha’s power is infinite; his body is universally at ease and reaches everywhere without exception. Thus he protects his own conduct, his body remains indestructible, and he acts according to his own will.
Firm and impartial, he subdues all things and enters them all universally; he perceives their causes, and his vision is pure.
Having transcended the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*), he practices the way of detachment, yet there is nothing he does not practice.

It is like empty space, tranquil and infinite; wherever it enters, there is neither acceptance nor non-acceptance—this is what is called merit, which is universally pervasive and great, reaching unto the state of profound serenity.
Just as space is free from peril and distress, so too do all bodhisattvas clearly understand their practice and enter into purity; their minds are equal to space, without any loss or impairment.
All Buddha-dharmas are like a vast ocean—extraordinary and limitless; there is that which one enters and dwells within, without interruption.

One enters all buddha-lands, establishing and guiding the multitudes of sentient beings across infinite realms. These are as bottomless as space, free from all material forms, and devoid of all sounds.

Observing that all beings universally manifest according to their conditions, he seeks to transform and guide them until they achieve full accomplishment; his resolve is as firm as space, incapable of being thwarted or defeated, and with a mind of such strength, he attains ultimate perfection.

The entire world is also like empty space, entirely devoid of anything substantial; that which is firm does not pursue the various worlds, eliminates all affection and craving, and is able to fulfill the Great Way.
In those kalpas, the heavens and earth are all consumed by fire until they are exhausted, yet empty space is not burned; empty space universally encompasses and receives all Buddha-worlds.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva enters into the various powers and establishes unsurpassed, true, and correct wisdom. This is what it means.
"This is the tenth Dharma-patience, wherein Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas realize that all dharmas are like emptiness.
When Samantabhadra Bodhisattva spoke this sutra, the assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, and humans, were all filled with joy.
